about: Pewabic Pottery, Detroit (1903 to today): eras, chronology, people, glazes and wares, installations, pieces in public collections, look-alikes. Built by hallmark-sources/pewabic/build_table.py in the website repo from the research there; marks are in marks/pewabic.json. Edit the research or edits.json, not this file.

eras.name: Stratton era, Stable Studio and Revelation period (before the Jefferson Avenue building)
eras.run_by: Mary Chase Perry (married W.B. Stratton in 1918) with partner Horace J. Caulkins, maker of the Revelation kiln; thrower Joseph Heerich; assistant Julius Albus
eras.made: Vases, bowls, candlesticks, jars and lamp bases, many with relief leaf decoration; the first commission was the 1903 Burley & Co. order of lamps, jars and other household wares
eras.marks: Hand-signed 'Perry' or 'MCP'; 'Revelation Pottery' with M.C.P.; a maple-leaf stamp with 'Pewabic'; paper labels. Pear and Catallo give the order of the early marks differently: see disagreements. The marks researcher owns the detail
eras.bodies_and_glazes: Matte glazes, mostly brown and green, with drips and crystalline spots. The the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination says that until 1907 pieces were 'hard white porcelain' with heavy opaque matte enamel; Barber 1904, as reported by Lehner, says 'hard white body'. No iridescent glazes yet
eras.how_to_tell: Pieces with Perry or MCP signatures, the Revelation seal or the maple-leaf stamp belong to this earliest period, and Pear calls them the 'earliest and rarest' work. A hard pale body with matte green or brown glaze and relief leaves fits this period, but matte green was also made later and is now reissued (see the modern era).
disagreements: Order of the early marks. Pear p.34: 'Perry', then Revelation/M.C.P., then the maple-leaf stamp, then the circular Pewabic seals. Evans (via Lehner p.342): Revelation for about a year before 1906, a maple leaf briefly, then the circle. Catallo pp.33-34: the circle first, then the large P over a small p, then the word Pewabic with maple leaves.
Year the name 'Pewabic' was adopted: 1903 (Catallo p.33; the National Historic Landmark nomination 1991) vs 1905 (Pear p.34) vs 1906 (Lehner p.342). This belongs to the history and marks researchers.
eras.label: The first workshop
eras.short: Mary Chase Perry's first workshop in a Detroit carriage house, firing in Horace Caulkins's Revelation kilns: thrown vases, bowls and lamp bases in heavy matte glazes, often with leaves in relief.
eras.run_by_short: Mary Chase Perry and Horace Caulkins

eras.name: Stratton era, Jefferson Avenue production pottery
eras.run_by: Mary Chase Perry Stratton until her death in 1961, with Caulkins until 1923; long-serving staff Julius Albus, Joseph Heerich, Joseph Ender, John Graziosi, Louis Tomasi; secretary Ella Peters from 1938
eras.made: Thrown vases, bowls and lamp bases; architectural tile on a large scale (churches, schools, libraries, homes, commercial buildings); in the Depression and wartime, small pieces such as jewelry, buttons, pins and earrings, cigarette boxes and ceramic postcards; a little dinnerware, mostly replacements for the Women's City Club. Wayne State University classes met in the building 1936-1947.
eras.marks: Impressed circular PEWABIC DETROIT stamps and variants; paper labels (tan, about 1 in., 'Pewabic' over 'Detroit'); a few pieces impressed 'Pewabic, Detroit, 1908'; large 2 in. seals with 'P.P.' on panels and garden pots. Charles Freer marked some pieces M1, M2 or M3 to note museum quality. Detail belongs to the marks researcher
eras.bodies_and_glazes: Low-fired, porous earthenware. Glazes were lead-based, and according to Pewabic's present glaze specialist some contained uranium. Iridescent glazes were developed from 1906 and perfected by 1909; the first iridescent sale is recorded on 12 April 1909. The iridescence forms in the glaze during firing rather than being painted on. Stratton never standardized forms or published catalogues.
eras.how_to_tell: Against modern Pewabic: (1) Body. Historic ware is soft, porous earthenware; modern giftware is high-fired white stoneware or porcelain. (2) Forming. Historic vessels were wheel-thrown by Heerich and others from Stratton's sketches; many modern heritage vases are slip-cast. (3) Finish. Pewabic's fabrication supervisor says today's product is 'more pristine' than in Stratton's time. (4) Mark. Modern pieces carry the current 'Pewabic logo' stamp, and at least one modern piece has a year in the stamp; Stratton-era pieces are generally undated. Genuine Stratton pieces may be unmarked: paper labels fall off and heavy glaze can hide the stamp.
disagreements: Stratton's death date: 16 March 1961 (Pear p.233, checked against the page image) vs 15 April 1961 (Catallo p.93). For the history researcher.
Whether Pewabic pieces were ever dated: Rago (pbs-ars-2013) had not seen dated pieces; Pear p.34 records Albion College pieces impressed 'Pewabic, Detroit, 1908'.
eras.label: The Jefferson Avenue pottery
eras.short: The pottery's own building on East Jefferson Avenue: thrown vases and bowls, the iridescent glazes from 1909, and architectural tile on a large scale for churches, schools, libraries, houses and office buildings.

eras.name: After Stratton: Ella Peters as manager, Henry Caulkins as owner
eras.run_by: Henry L. Caulkins, Horace's son, sole owner after inheriting Stratton's shares; Ella (Mrs. Ira) Peters, Stratton's secretary since 1938, as general manager
eras.made: Orders continued. Peters completed Stratton's final installations, and the pottery still filled commercial orders: Pear lists commissions for 1962 (Lambda Theta, Ann Arbor; Jewish Community Center), 1963 (Chevrolet office; Hiram Walker, Windsor), 1964 (Grosse Pointe Farms City Hall) and 1966 (Zonta Club; Hamilton Center, State of Michigan). Pear also notes Pewabic designed State of Michigan seals in 1931 and again in 1962. Pewabic's timeline says Peters 'oversaw everyday production'. A Roadshow guest said Ira Peters 'worked at the pottery in the '60s' and made pieces, one inscribed 'Elisabeth Christmas', apparently dated '66. Kovels reportedly says the Peterses kept making pottery with Pewabic glazes in a home studio until 1969.
eras.marks: Not documented. No source found that describes a mark specific to 1961-1969 work. A Cranbrook record, seen only as a search snippet, reportedly dates the circular PEWABIC DETROIT mark 'circa 1910 until 1967' (lead, unverified).
eras.bodies_and_glazes: Not documented separately; presumably the same materials and glazes, but no source says so.
eras.how_to_tell: No documented way to tell 1961-1969 work from late Stratton work. Clues that a piece is post-Stratton: a personal inscription or a 1960s date (the Roadshow '66 piece), or provenance to the Peters family. This is thin; treat it as a gap.
disagreements: End of Peters-run production: 1965 (a Freer Gallery bowl record, F1917.432, as seen in a search snippet: 'until it closed in 1965'; unverified, page blocked); 1966 (fisher-2003 p.75; brunk-2007; nps-nhl-1991 'continued its production of ceramic ware until 1966'); February 1969, the last Day Book entry (pear-1976 pp.231, 233); home studio until 1969 (kovels-pewabic snippet).
Peters' tenure: Pear says she joined in 1938 (p.231); Pewabic's timeline says 37 years; Rago (pbs-ars-2013) says 'at least 30 years'.
eras.label: After Mrs. Stratton
eras.short: Henry Caulkins, Horace's son, owned the pottery and Ella Peters, Mrs. Stratton's secretary since 1938, managed it, finishing the commissions on hand while production wound down.

eras.name: Michigan State University years
eras.run_by: Michigan State University: Continuing Education to 1976, then University Extension to 1981. Director Roger Ault by the late 1970s; adult classes taught by James Powell (Cranbrook MFA). Henry Caulkins gave the building and contents; the deed was registered 21 Dec 1967
eras.made: An education center, not a production pottery. Catallo says Michigan State ownership effectively ended 'more than a half century's worth of production pottery'; the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination calls it a 'classroom facility'. Classes earned university credit. Exhibitions and shows: an invitational Christmas show of 20 area potters (1974) and Jim Powell's salt-glazed pottery (1976). Primo Valoni was photographed in Pewabic's kiln room around 1969. No source documents Pewabic-branded production for sale in these years.
eras.marks: Not found. No source describes an Michigan State-era Pewabic mark, or whether student or instructor work made in the building was stamped.
eras.how_to_tell: Nothing documented. Things an owner should know: (1) Pewabic did not run a production line in these years, so a 'Pewabic' piece made 1967-1981 is likely student, instructor or guest-artist work, or old stock; that is an inference from the sources above. (2) Historic material left the building: archives and artifacts went missing, and historic pieces from the attic were dispersed in a 1978 sale, so Stratton-era pieces with 'from the pottery' provenance can come from this route.
disagreements: Start year: 1965 (brunk-2007: 'gave the pottery to Michigan State University in 1965'); 1966 (msu-ua339; lehner-1988 p.342 'around 1966'; nps-nhl-1991 production 'until 1966'); 1967 (pewabic-timeline; pewabic-blog-msu-2019; pewabic-blog-vessels-2026; catallo-2017 p.94; Pewabic's Michigan State ornament text; Pear's deed registered 21 Dec 1967).
Pear (p.233) has the pottery 'filling orders' under Peters until February 1969, overlapping the Michigan State deed (1967). Lehner says Michigan State had it 'operating again' by 1968.
eras.label: Michigan State University
eras.short: Michigan State University held the building as a teaching center: classes and exhibitions, not production.

eras.name: Pewabic Society: modern Pewabic
eras.run_by: The Pewabic Society, Inc. (nonprofit, formed 1979; 'Friends of Pewabic' in Pewabic's timeline), owner from 1 Sep 1981. Early leaders include David McKeehan (Society president)
eras.made: Production resumed in 1982 or 1983 (see disagreements); the education studio opened in 1983. Output since then: architectural tile (People Mover stations 1986-87, Comerica Park 2000, QLine 2017, restorations); giftware vessels, tiles, ornaments and jewelry. Many are reissues of Stratton-era designs, and the shop also sells other artists' work. The vessel studio moved to the 'Firehouse' across Jefferson Avenue in 2005, and a 2,500 sq ft tile studio addition followed in 2018-19.
eras.marks: Pewabic's shop says every current piece has the 'Pewabic logo stamped on back' (tiles and ornaments) or 'stamped on the bottom' (vessels). A documented 1992 example reads, in circles, 'JFM' (maker's initials) and '[leaf] PEWABIC / 1992 / DETROIT'. Hand-painted modern tiles (Postcards series, Historic Peacock hand-painted, Nekhbet) are 'signed by a Pewabic artist'. The shop text does not say whether the year still appears in today's stamp.
eras.bodies_and_glazes: White stoneware for thrown and cast vessels and for tile ('formulated to closely match the appearance of our tile'); porcelain for many small pressed pieces (ornaments, pins, some tiles); 'High-fire stoneware'. Firing: oxidation firings just above 2200 to 2260 F; copper red up to about 2310 F. Glazes: lead-free and reformulated, with more than 600 variations; the giftware palette uses fewer than 20 colors and architecture about 70. Modern iridescent glazes take a third firing with 'fuming' (vegetable oil injected into the kiln) and are 'soft' (no flower food). The clay body and glazes were reformulated after Custer feldspar ran out in 2023.
eras.how_to_tell: Modern Pewabic is told apart by (1) the current Pewabic logo stamp, sometimes with a year and maker's initials, or an artist's signature on hand-painted tiles; (2) a hard, high-fired white stoneware or porcelain body rather than porous earthenware; (3) slip-cast vases in historic designs, listed in the Heritage Collection; and (4) a more uniform, 'pristine' finish [sources as cited]. Caution: The Henry Ford catalogues its 1992 vase as 'Earthenware', so the switch to stoneware is undated.

sources.where: 'Is everything in the store made at Pewabic?'

disagreements: Production restart: 1982 (nps-nhl-1991 'the following year') vs 1983 (pewabic-timeline; pewabic-blog-vessels-2026; catallo-2017 p.98: 'In December 1983, the transition was complete').
Society formation: 1979 (msu-ua339; pewabic-timeline; catallo-2017 p.96; brunk-2007) vs 'In 1981, the nonprofit Pewabic Society was incorporated' (fisher-2003 p.75).
Modern body: The Henry Ford catalogues the 1992 vase as earthenware; Pewabic's 2026 posts and shop describe white stoneware and porcelain. The changeover year is not documented.
eras.label: Pewabic today
eras.short: The nonprofit Pewabic Society runs the pottery. Production of pottery and tile started again in 1982 or 1983: architectural tile and public art, giftware, and reissues of Mrs. Stratton's designs, beside classes.

name.claim: Named after the Pewabic copper mine (lode) at Hancock, Perry's birthplace
Pewabic means 'clay with a copper color' (the meaning Perry herself repeated)
Pewabic is the Ojibwe word biwabik / biiwaabik, 'iron' or 'metal' - not 'copper' or 'clay'
Named after the region of Upper Michigan associated with her birthplace
Who chose it: Perry put 'Pewabic' on a list (with Valor, Starbright, Hamtramck, Orion) and Frank Burley of Burley & Co. picked it as an American 'Indian' word

founding.claim: about 1899 ('established some seventeen years ago' in 1916)
1901 (stable rented fall 1901; first exhibition 1901; 'opened ... Pewabic Pottery in Detroit in 1901')
1903 (name adopted with the Burley order; the year the pottery itself uses)
about 1903 ('her past two year's quiet work', Feb. 1905)
about 1906 ('founded in Detroit about 20 years ago', 1926)
1907 (the Golden Anniversary of 1957 counts from the Jefferson Avenue building)

events.text: Horace James Caulkins born at Oshawa, Ontario.
disagreements: Detroit Historical Society (dhs-caulkins) gives July 25, 1850: 'born in Oshawa, Ontario, on July 25th, 1850'.

events.text: The Pewabic amygdaloid lode near Hancock opened (Pewabic and Quincy Mining Company); the Pewabic mine is the usual source given for the pottery's name.
disagreements: Year from Pear only ('Early in 1852 the Portage Lake amygdaloid district opened'); the mine's history was not researched further (see Quincy Mining Co. The National Historic Landmark nomination documentation).

events.text: Charles Lang Freer, later Pewabic's patron, born at Kingston, New York.
William Buck Stratton, architect of the pottery and later Perry's husband, born.
disagreements: Pear: Newfield, NY, Feb. 16, 1865 (checked against page image).
Catallo: Ithaca, NY, 1864 (checked against page image); Catallo also has him 73 at death in May 1938, consistent with 1864/65.
NR nomination for the Stratton House (nr-stratton-house-1984, Item 8) gives 'William Buck Stratton (1867-1938)'.

events.text: The copper steamer PEWABIC sinks in Lake Huron after colliding with the Meteor. Pear says the name's association came from the Pewabic mine and 'a boat of that name'.
Mary Chase Perry born in Hancock, Michigan, in the Keweenaw copper country, second daughter of Dr. William Walbridge Perry and Sophia (Sophie) Barrett Perry.
disagreements: Pear's sentence is grammatically ambiguous (the Civil War ended in 1865), but it can only mean a birth date of March 15, 1867; Catallo and the Detroit Historical Society state it plainly.
events.short: Mary Chase Perry born in Hancock, in Michigan’s copper country

events.text: Dr. W. W. Perry assaulted at night by a passenger put off the train, never recovered and died the following spring; the family moved to Ann Arbor.
disagreements: Year of death: 1877 (Detroit Historical Society, The Henry Ford, Pewabic history page) vs. spring 1878 implied by Pear and Catallo ('died the following spring' after an 1877 attack).
Her age: ten (Pear p. 10; Fisher p. 73) vs. thirteen (the National Historic Landmark nomination 1991 Sec. 8 p. 3: 'After her father's death when she was thirteen').

events.text: Family moves from Ann Arbor to Detroit and rents a furnished house on Edmund Place (Brush Park) next door to the Horace J. Caulkins family.
disagreements: Pear p. 11: when Mary Chase was twelve (about 1879); Catallo: when she was thirteen (about 1880). No source gives the exact year.

events.text: Studies at the Art Academy of Cincinnati, 1887-1889 (clay modelling and sculpture; Catallo names the sculptor Louis Rebisso).
A year at the Detroit Museum of Art school, then china-painting teaching in Asheville, North Carolina.
disagreements: The Henry Ford dates the Asheville studio to summer 1891 ('when she purchased a portable kiln and set up a studio in Asheville'); single-source for that date.

events.text: Opens a china-painting studio at 6 West Adams, Detroit, with three other young women.
Perry begins demonstrating and selling Caulkins' Revelation china kilns (made by H. J. Caulkins & Co., Detroit) across the country; the start of the Perry-Caulkins partnership.
disagreements: NR Stratton House nomination (1984): 'As early as 1897 she began working with Horace J. Caulkins'.
events.short: She begins selling and demonstrating Horace Caulkins’s Revelation kilns

events.text: Portable kerosene-fired muffle kiln, made for Caulkins (the Revelation kiln), patented; parts made by Egle Bros., Detroit.
disagreements: Only Catallo gives the patent date (checked against page image); the patent itself was not looked up. Who designed the original dental kiln (Caulkins or the dentist Dr. Charles Land) is disputed (Catallo p. 20).

events.text: Perry and Caulkins open an experimental workshop (according to the 1991 the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination, citing Brunk 1976).
disagreements: See the 'Stable Studio opens' entries: other sources put the first workshop in 1900, 1901, 1903 or 1904.

events.text: Perry spends three weeks at the first summer school of the New York State School of Clay-Working and Ceramics, Alfred, under Charles F. Binns (with Marshal Fry teaching overglaze).
disagreements: Catallo p. 28: three weeks 'in 1901' with Marshal Fry and Charles F. Binns.

The National Historic Landmark nomination 1991 Sec. 8 p. 4: 'In 1901 and 1902, Perry studied glaze chemistry at Alfred University under Charles Binns'; NR Stratton House 1984: 'under Charles Binns at Alfred University 1901-02'.
Period evidence: Keramic Studio Oct. 1902 p. 120 shows 'Vase Glazed by Mary Chase Perry' among work of the Alfred summer school, so she was at Alfred in summer 1902 too.

events.text: The 'Stable Studio' (also 'Miss Perry's Pottery', 'Revelation Pottery', 'Stable Pottery'): a vacant carriage house/stable on Alfred Street at John R, Brush Park, owned by Alanson Fox, leased at $8 a month payable quarterly; Julius Albus, aged 12, becomes the first employee.
disagreements: Year the stable was taken: 1900 (Pewabic timeline); fall 1901 (The Henry Ford: 'In the fall of 1901 ... she arranged to rent and renovate an unused carriage house'); 1898 workshop (the National Historic Landmark nomination 1991); 1901 (NR Stratton House 1984: 'opened the internationally known Pewabic Pottery in Detroit in 1901'); 1903 (Fisher p. 73; Detroit Historical Society; Lehner p. 342 'Around 1903'); 1904 (NR 1971: 'set up her first pottery in an abandoned stable in Detroit in 1904').

Pear p. 23 says the lease was made in 'late fall' without a year; Pear p. 171 puts the first exhibition in the Stable-Studio in 1901, and p. 206 has Albus starting there in 1901. Pear's Fig. 13 caption dates the Stable-Studio '1903-1907'.
Catallo and Pear say the lease and Albus' hiring, not the year, so Pear's 1901 for Albus (checked against page image) is the earliest dated event at the stable in Pear.
events.short: The first workshop, in a carriage house on Alfred Street (the sources date it from 1898 to 1904)

events.text: Perry listed in Keramic Studio at 44 Gratiot Avenue, Detroit, the address of Caulkins' kiln company (H. J. Caulkins & Co., 44-46 Gratiot Avenue).
Revelation Kiln No. 3 unveiled for studio potters; Perry makes demonstration pieces stamped 'Revelation Pottery'.
First exhibition of the pottery's work, held in the Stable-Studio, when its products were known as 'Miss Perry's Pottery'.
Julius Albus, aged twelve, goes to work at the Stable-Studio (first employee).
disagreements: Year single-source (Pear, checked against page image); Pewabic timeline implies 1900 ('soon afterward').

events.text: Perry and Caulkins in New York making pottery and underglaze-firing experiments with the new Revelation kiln (at Mrs. Poillon's New York School of Pottery).
Freer shows Perry an iridescent (Syrian/ancient) piece and challenges her to recreate the luster.
disagreements: The National Historic Landmark nomination 1991 Sec. 8 p. 6: 'In 1903 Perry's friend, art collector Charles Lang Freer, urged her to try to recreate the iridescent glazes'.

events.text: Joseph Heerich, an Alsatian-trained thrower found cleaning Pullman cars at the Michigan Central depot, hired to throw Perry's drawn shapes, first in the evenings (7-10 pm), later full time.
disagreements: Catallo: Heerich reached Detroit 'around 1902' and went full time 'within roughly two years'.
Pewabic timeline puts his hiring in 1903 ('This same year, a second employee was added to the roster - Joseph Heerich').
The Henry Ford: 'By the end of 1903, Perry had hired a professional potter'.
Keramic Studio Feb. 1905 p. 218 mentions 'one man to throw the forms on the wheel' but names no one; no period source names Heerich.

events.text: Burley & Company, Chicago, orders $1,000 worth of bowls and lamp jars; at Burley's urging the ware gets a trade name, Pewabic, after the Pewabic copper mine near her Hancock birthplace.
disagreements: Pear p. 34 contradicts her own p. 28: '"Pewabic Pottery" became the official name in 1905' after a visit to Burley 'in 1905'.
Detroit Historical Society: partnership and Stable Studio in 1903, 'The following year, they renamed the business Pewabic Pottery' (i.e. 1904).

Lehner p. 342: 'in 1906 a new pottery was built on Jefferson Avenue, and the name became Pewabic Pottery' - contradicted by period print: the name appears in Keramic Studio Feb. 1904 and in Barber 1904.
Catallo p. 32 lists the other names on Perry's list: Valor, Starbright, Hamtramck, Orion.
events.short: A first large order, from Burley & Company of Chicago, and the name Pewabic

events.text: First Burley order recorded in the books: 132 pieces totalling $1,068.10, payment received.
disagreements: Pear reproduces Day Book pages for Burley orders of 1903 and 1904 (Pear p. 22 and p. 24 captions, PDF 26 and 28) without these totals.

events.text: Pewabic pottery shown in the Michigan Building at the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, St. Louis. No award to Perry or Pewabic found.
disagreements: Pear Fig. 357 (p. 172) captions a shipment 'sent to the World's Fair Exhibition at St. Louis' as 'May 21, 1905'; the fair closed Dec. 1, 1904, so the caption date is doubtful.
Perry/Pewabic are absent from the Department of Art (Group XIV) awards list (illustrationsse00loui); other departments' award lists were not searched.

events.text: Earliest printed use of the name found: Keramic Studio notes 'the new Pewabic art pottery made by Miss Mary Chase Perry', fired in the large Revelation pottery kiln.
Mary Chase Perry's Pewabic pottery shown at the First Annual Exhibition of Arts and Crafts, Detroit Museum of Art, Dec. 6-20, 1904.

Keramic Studio profile 'Mary Chase Perry, Potter': her 'past two year's quiet work'; three helpers only (Caulkins, a thrower, a young boy); ware named from 'an Indian river near Miss Perry's home'; photo 'Home of the Pewabic Pottery'.
disagreements: Catallo repeats the Keramic Studio article, so the two count as one.

events.text: Detroit Society of Arts and Crafts founded; Perry, Caulkins and William B. Stratton among the founders (Stratton vice-president, George G. Booth president).
Architects Stratton & Baldwin (William B. Stratton and Frank C. Baldwin) commissioned to design a purpose-built pottery on East Jefferson Avenue, modelled on a Kentish inn.
disagreements: Pear p. 30 says Caulkins, 'being of English descent', wanted the old English inn type 'from the Kent district'.

events.text: Collection of Pewabic Pottery (no. 515) exhibited at the Architectural League of New York's 21st annual exhibition.
New York Society of Keramic Arts exhibition: a wall of Pewabic tiles in matte glazes.

The new pottery at 2161 Jefferson Avenue (now 10125 East Jefferson) is built and production moves in; the building was opened with a luncheon for Charles L. Freer and Prof. Arthur W. Dow of Teachers College, Columbia.
disagreements: 1906 vs 1907: Lehner p. 342 'which had been built in 1906' and 'in 1906 a new pottery was built on Jefferson Avenue'; Pewabic Society fact sheet 1991 'built in 1906-7'; the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination itself has design in 1906 (Sec. 8 p. 5) and 'designed and built ... in 1907' (Sec. 7).

1907 vs 1908: NR 1971 (Michigan Historical Commission) 'By 1908, the Pottery had moved to new quarters'; Michigan SHPO page '1907-08, building constructed'; Plumb (Jan. 1911) 'three years ago a simple plaster and wood building ... was erected'.
Pear p. 60 and p. 233: Caulkins paid $5,000 for the two lots on Sept. 29, 1907 (checked against page image), which sits awkwardly with a 1906 design; it may be a deed or final-payment date.
Pear's Day Book year in the new building starts November 1907 (p. 160).
The 1957 'Golden Anniversary' (Pear p. 260) counts from 1907.
events.short: The pottery moves into its own building on East Jefferson Avenue

events.text: Society of Arts and Crafts, Boston, exhibition: Mary Chase Perry, Detroit, nos. 1042-1049.
Caulkins pays $5,000 for the two Jefferson Avenue lots (50 ft of Lot E and 30 ft of Lot D, Water Works Subdivision, Private Claim 257).
disagreements: Pear gives it twice; no deed seen.

events.text: First Day Book year in the new building (Nov. 1907-Nov. 1908); 53 different workers recorded Nov. 1907-Dec. 1913.
Architectural League of America convention in Detroit visits the pottery's 'quaint building, designed by Architects Stratton & Baldwin'.
Work begins on tile for St. Paul's Cathedral (Episcopal), Detroit, architect Ralph Adams Cram; Pewabic won the floor-tile contract in open competition.
disagreements: Belongs mainly to the installations topic.
events.short: Tile for St. Paul’s Cathedral, Detroit, its first great church commission

events.text: Pewabic Pottery advertised at '2161 JEFFERSON-AVE.', opposite the Detroit Water Works, M. C. Perry and H. J. Caulkins.
First successful iridescent glaze opened from the kiln; first recorded iridescent sale to Freer, May 1, 1909.
disagreements: Catallo p. 59: 'in probably 1906' Perry presented Freer with a red iridescent bowl; she notes other accounts give 1909 and Jacqueline Peck (Detroit Women's City Club Magazine, April 1952) gives 1910.
Pewabic timeline: after '4 years and countless trials' from Freer's 1902 challenge (about 1906).
Period: Handicraft June 1910 p. 114 calls 'the new Pewabic lustre' of special interest.
The National Historic Landmark nomination's 1909 statement cites Brunk 1976, not Pear, so Pear and the National Historic Landmark nomination are independent here.
events.short: The first iridescent glaze comes from the kiln; Charles Lang Freer buys the first piece on May 1

events.text: Louis Tomasi, an Italian potter trained in the Tyrol (Austria), starts work at Pewabic.
Horace and Minnie Caulkins deed a one-half interest in the Jefferson Avenue property to Mary Chase Perry (warranty deed).
Hotel Griswold (Postal's) bar room, Detroit, finished entirely in Pewabic pottery tile.
disagreements: Installations topic; Catallo notes a postcard of the bar postmarked Feb. 1911.

events.text: Freer's house fireplace (East Ferry Avenue) tiled with early Pewabic iridescent tiles.
Plans for an addition to the plant of the Pewabic Pottery Co. by Stratton & Baldwin; a two-story factory addition planned.

Rear addition built: clay-making equipment (blunger, filter press, pug mill/clay mixer still in use), tile pressing, glazing and upstairs layout space. Pewabic calls it the only expansion of production space until 2018-19.
disagreements: Pear records building-addition costs for 1911-1912 without a completion date.

events.text: Joseph Ender, Heerich's nephew from Germany, starts work (kilns, blunger, grog, glaze mills).
disagreements: 1912 (Pear, image-checked) vs 1911 (Catallo, image-checked).

events.text: Freer buys fourteen pieces in one purchase.
disagreements: Freer accession records were not reachable (Smithsonian sites block automated reading); see corpus topic.

events.text: Pewabic stops making lamps.
Freer presents three selected pieces of Pewabic Pottery and an ebony table to the Detroit Museum of Art.
Pewabic Pottery 'made under the direction of Mary Chase Perry' shown at the Handicraft Club exhibition, Peabody Institute, Baltimore.
Honorable Mention for 'a group of vases and tiles' at the American Federation of Arts Exhibition of American Industrial Art, U.S. National Museum, Washington (May 17-June 17, 1916).
disagreements: Pear's own captions date the Washington show both 'May 12, 1916' (Fig. 362) and 'May 12, 1915' (Fig. 365).

events.text: Loan of 26 pieces of Pewabic pottery to the Detroit Museum of Art.
Group of Pewabic Pottery presented to the Detroit Museum of Art by Perry and Caulkins.
Pewabic luster tiles shown at the Society of Arts and Crafts, Boston, pottery exhibition.
Mary Chase Perry marries William Buck Stratton at the home of Horace J. Caulkins, 188 Parker Avenue, Detroit.

sources.where: p. 366 (May 1918 report still calls her 'Miss Perry')

disagreements: NPS Places page and Arts & Crafts Homes (web) say 1917; Fisher p. 73 says 'Eleven years later' than the 1907 building, i.e. 1918. Period: Book of Detroiters 1914 lists Stratton 'unmarried' and American Magazine of Art July 1918 still calls her 'Miss Perry' in a May 1918 report.
events.short: She marries William Buck Stratton, the pottery’s architect

events.text: Charles Lang Freer dies.
disagreements: Day from Pear only.

events.text: Fire in the rear of the Pewabic building; trade press reports $36,000 damage to the two-story building at Hurlbut and Jefferson.
disagreements: Day from Pear only.

events.text: Mr. and Mrs. Frank G. Logan medal (and $100) at the Art Institute of Chicago's 20th annual exhibition of applied arts.
disagreements: Pear reproduces an award letter dated Oct. 11, 1921 (Fig. 371).

events.text: Horace James Caulkins dies; buried in Elmwood Cemetery, Detroit, under a monument Perry Stratton designed. His half of the business passes to his widow Minnie.
disagreements: Exact date not found. Period: Art and Archaeology, Mar. 1924, p. 113 refers to 'the late Horace J. Caulkins'.
Catallo p. 93 says that at her death Perry Stratton had 'outlived her business partner by twenty-nine years' - an arithmetic slip (1961-1923 = 38).

events.text: The Strattons sail for Portugal, Spain and Italy to study early Christian and Islamic work for the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception crypt commission (contract signed Feb. 1924). Julius Albus left in charge.
disagreements: NR 1971 dates the Shrine commission 'In 1925'. Catallo: letter to Charles Maginnis Feb. 23, 1924, contract two days later.

events.text: Minnie Peck Caulkins gives her one-half interest in the pottery to her son Henry L. Caulkins; she remains largely a silent partner.
disagreements: Catallo p. 93 says Henry 'had inherited his mother's stake'; Pewabic timeline says he 'had already inherited his father's part of the business'.

events.text: The Strattons build their house at 938 Three Mile Drive, Grosse Pointe Park (reusing material from 138 East Grand Boulevard); Gwen Lux and Alexis Lapteff live there as resident artists.
disagreements: Pear p. 143 says the house was built in 1928, and p. 81 that they lived at 138 East Grand Boulevard 'until 1928'.

events.text: Pewabic Pottery incorporated as a stock company: Mary Chase Stratton president (51 percent), Minnie Peck Caulkins vice-president, Henry L. Caulkins secretary-treasurer.
disagreements: Pear p. 60 names Ruth Stone Caulkins, not Minnie, as vice-president, citing a warranty deed of June 1, 1929.

events.text: University of Michigan confers an honorary Master of Arts on Mary Chase Stratton.
disagreements: Day from Catallo only.

events.text: Honorary Doctor of Science from the Colleges of the City of Detroit (later Wayne State University).
disagreements: Pewabic timeline: 'She received an honorary Ph.D. from Wayne State University in 1932'.

events.text: Wayne (Colleges of the City of Detroit) ceramics classes held at the Pewabic building, Friday evenings and Saturday mornings, 1936-1947.
disagreements: Catallo gives no years; she reports Murray Douglas' view that the classes were offered for tax relief. The 1991 Pewabic Society fact sheet says she 'established the Ceramics Departments at Wayne State and the University of Michigan'.

events.text: Mrs. Stratton buys the Revelation kiln molds, patterns, fixtures and rights from Egle Brothers, Detroit (contract witnessed by Julius Albus).
disagreements: Pear gives both June 13 and June 15, 1936 (OCR; not image-checked).

events.text: The Strattons give up the Three Mile Drive house to keep the pottery open, moving back to East Grand Boulevard (Pear: no. 134, 1937-1945).
Joseph Heerich, master thrower, dies at 85 at the home of his nephew Joseph Ender, 1161 Holcomb, Detroit.
disagreements: Pear's chapter heading (p. 210) reads 'Joseph Heerich 1853-1937' (image-checked). The Catallo OCR file reads '1958' - an OCR error; the page image says 1938.

events.text: Ella Peters (née Pomella) joins as office secretary and bookkeeper.
disagreements: Pear p. 207 says Albus was general supervisor 'until 1940 when Mrs. Ella Peters was engaged as secretary'. Pewabic timeline calls her 'bookkeeper and secretary of 37 years'.

events.text: William Buck Stratton dies in hospital after being struck by a streetcar.
disagreements: May 12 (Pear) vs May 14 (Catallo), both checked against page images. Catallo's bibliography cites a Detroit Free Press obituary of 14 May 1938, which would fit a death on May 12 or 13 better than May 14 - not checked.

events.text: Mary Chase Stratton under contract to the University of Michigan as Lecturer on Ceramics (1940-1942), part of the Earhart-funded creative arts work; she set up U-M's ceramics studio.
disagreements: Pear dates the contract June 15, 1940 (single-source). Catallo: Emil Lorch first asked her to teach on Sept. 18, 1933.

events.text: Her textbook Ceramic Processes published (Edwards Brothers, Ann Arbor).
disagreements: 1941 (Pear p. 240) vs 1946 (Pear p. 183); Catallo's bibliography lists both 1941 and 1946, which suggests two printings. Not checked against a library record.

events.text: Her article 'Pewabic Records' published in the Bulletin of the American Ceramic Society (vol. 25 no. 10, Oct. 15, 1946, pp. 364-365).
Charles Fergus Binns Medal (New York State College of Ceramics, Alfred), presented at Atlantic City.
Julius Albus, supervisor and last of the original Stable-Studio staff, dies aged 62.
disagreements: Pear says 'forty-five years' of service; 1901-1951 is fifty.

events.text: First Detroit Institute of Arts retrospective of her work.
John Graziosi, thrower for 47 years, dies.
Golden Anniversary of the pottery (counted from 1907) marked by a banquet at the Statler Hotel; Mrs. Stratton present at 90.
Joseph Ender, kiln man since 1911/12, dies aged 74.

Henry L. Caulkins, Horace's son, inherits her shares (she willed her 51 percent to him) and becomes the pottery's first sole owner; Ella Peters stays on as manager and finishes the last installations.
Louis Tomasi dies.
disagreements: Pear's heading not image-checked.

events.text: Mary Chase Perry Stratton dies in Detroit, aged 94; buried at Greenwood Cemetery, Birmingham, Michigan, near W. B. Stratton.
disagreements: Pear contradicts herself: p. 261 'until her death, March 16, 1961' and p. 233 'March [16,] 1961'; p. 230 'Mrs. Stratton's death in March, 1961'. All image-checked where quoted.
April 15 is given by Pear's list of legal records and by Catallo (who used Pear, so not fully independent). No obituary was found to settle it.
events.short: Mary Chase Perry Stratton dies in Detroit, aged 94

events.text: Henry L. Caulkins gives the pottery to Michigan State University, which runs it through its continuing-education/extension service as a ceramics teaching satellite with galleries for the Pewabic collection; production pottery effectively ends.

sources.where: fact sheet (the National Historic Landmark nomination file)

disagreements: 1965: Pewabic's own history page, 'The pottery was gifted to Michigan State University in 1965'.

1966: NR 1971 (image-checked), Pewabic Society 1991, the National Historic Landmark nomination 1991, Fisher p. 75 (Ella Peters ran it 'until 1966', then 'Bequeathed to Michigan State University by the Caulkins family').
Start of 1967: Catallo p. 94 'By the start of 1967, Pewabic had opened its doors as property of Michigan State' (image-checked).

1967: Pewabic timeline 'Michigan State opened the pottery once more in 1967'; Pear p. 233 'In 1967 the deed ... was given to the Board of Trustees of Michigan State University and registered on December 21 of that year'; Pear p. 60 'December 21, 1967' (image-checked).
1968: Lehner p. 342 'By 1968 it was operating again'.

Gift or sale: Lehner p. 342 says Henry Caulkins 'purchased the pottery and put it under the care of the Michigan State University' - not supported; every other source has Henry already the owner (from 1961) and giving it ('donated', 'deeded', 'gifted', 'in honor of his father').
Ella Peters' last Day Book entry is February 1969 (Pear p. 231), so some orders continued past 1966.
events.short: Henry Caulkins gives the pottery to Michigan State University

events.text: C. Allan Harlan, Detroit industrialist and former Michigan State trustee, gives $35,000 toward rehabilitating the building; Michigan State president John Hannah accepts the gift.
Deed of Pewabic Pottery to the Board of Trustees of Michigan State University recorded, given by Henry L. Caulkins in honor of his father.
disagreements: See the 1966 Michigan State entry for the competing dates.

events.text: James (Jim) Powell, Cranbrook-trained potter, becomes instructor at Michigan State's Pewabic; daily adult-education classes.
disagreements: Year from Lehner only.

events.text: Ella Peters makes the last entry in the Day Book: 'Goodbye, my job ends.'
disagreements: Fisher p. 75 says Peters directed the pottery 'until 1966'.

events.text: Listed on the Michigan State Register of Historic Sites (Pear: Michigan Historic Site no. 92); National Register nomination prepared Nov. 13, 1970 by Jim Schutze, Michigan Historical Commission.
disagreements: Pear p. 233 credits 'this author's applications' (Pear herself) for the state and national listings.

events.text: Pewabic Pottery entered in the National Register of Historic Places (owner: Michigan State University).
disagreements: HistoricDetroit.org says 'Sep. 4, 1971'.

events.text: Thomas W. Brunk becomes curator and archivist of Michigan State University's Pewabic Pottery (to 1981).
Large Pewabic exhibition at the Freer Gallery of Art.
disagreements: Catallo's bibliography lists Bleicher, Hu and Uren, Highlights of Pewabic Pottery (Michigan State and Ars Ceramica, 1977), probably related; not seen.

events.text: Michigan State moves to close the pottery at the end of fiscal year 1979; director Roger Ault and Mary Jane Hock (Detroit Council of the Arts) rally support; Henry S. Booth offers $5,000 (letter of Oct. 18, 1978); closing postponed.

The nonprofit Pewabic Society (first 'Friends of Pewabic') is formed to subsidize Michigan State's running costs and save the pottery; Thomas W. Brunk a co-founder; David McKeehan its president during the transfer.
disagreements: Fisher p. 75: 'In 1981, the nonprofit Pewabic Society was incorporated' (incorporation, not founding, may be the difference). The National Historic Landmark nomination 1991 calls it 'the newly formed Pewabic Society' in 1981.

events.text: Michigan State University transfers the pottery to the 200-member Pewabic Society (deadline was the end of Michigan State's fiscal year, June 30, 1981; dean Raymond Vlasin).
disagreements: Day (Sept. 1) from Catallo only (image-checked).

Gift vs sale: Lehner p. 342 cites 'Pewabic Pottery Sold', American Art Pottery, Nov. 1981, p. 4 ('sold to the Pewabic Society, Inc. because of budget cutbacks'); Catallo quotes an Michigan State dean offering to 'give it to you'. Terms not found.
events.short: Michigan State hands the pottery to the nonprofit Pewabic Society

events.text: Production of architectural tile revived; first commission of the new era for WDIV-TV (1982-83); attic converted to studio space under a grant written by David McKeehan.
disagreements: Pewabic timeline puts the return to production in 1983 ('Back to its roots'); Catallo: 'In December 1983, the transition was complete', followed by the People Mover commission.

events.text: Education studio created on the second floor in the space called 'The Loft'.
Mary Chase Perry Stratton inducted (posthumously) into the Michigan Women's Hall of Fame.
Four major public art works for the Detroit People Mover stations made and installed, 1986-87.
disagreements: Installations topic.

events.text: National Historic Landmark nomination prepared (Jill S. Topolski, June 12, 1991; site visit Feb. 1991). Society officers then: Virginia Ryan, president; interim executive director Ronald Streitz, Jr.; archivist Melanie Bazil.
Designated a National Historic Landmark by the Secretary of the Interior (period of significance 1907-1941; the National Historic Landmark nomination criteria 1 and 2; theme Decorative and Folk Art).
Pewabic's centennial year (counted from 1903).
disagreements: The 1957 Golden Anniversary counted from 1907 (Pear p. 260), so the pottery has used two founding years for anniversaries.

events.text: Alex Thullen joins as glaze development specialist.
The building's chimney restored.
Steve McBride, a former studio potter at Pewabic, executive director (about 2015 to Sept. 30, 2025); Knight Arts Challenge grant buys a van for a mobile pottery program (2015).
disagreements: Start year inferred from 'a decade'; no announcement of his appointment was found.

events.text: Fund-raising announced for a 2,500 sq ft tile-studio addition behind the historic building.
The Maxine and Stuart Frankel Foundation Pewabic Tile Studio (2,500 sq ft, $1.1 million; built 2018, opened 2019) - described by Pewabic as the first expansion of production space since 1912.
disagreements: Both Pewabic pages are the maker's own account; Catallo confirms the plan only.

events.text: Pewabic installs a memorial grave marker at Mary Chase Perry Stratton's grave, Historic Greenwood Cemetery, Birmingham, Michigan.
Jim Leija (formerly Deputy Director and 2025 Acting Director, University of Michigan Museum of Art) named executive director; begins July 1, 2026. Board chair David Fox.
disagreements: An interim executive director served between McBride's departure and Leija; a search snippet names Dayna Deaner, but Pewabic's board page could not be opened (bot check).

people.name: Mary Chase Perry Stratton
people.life: b. 15 Mar 1867 Hancock, Mich.; d. 15 Apr 1961 (Pear p. 60, Catallo p. 93) or 16 Mar 1961 (Pear p. 261), Detroit
people.role: Founder, artist, designer and glaze chemist; ran the pottery until her death
people.notes: She drew the shapes and pinned them above the wheel for the thrower (Heerich), trimmed and decorated leather-hard pieces, and did the glazing; 'she uses no moulds' (Keramic Studio 1905). Signed 'Perry' or 'MCP' on early pieces (Pear p. 34). Pear p. 161: products bore Pewabic seals, not individual potters' names.

people.name: Horace James Caulkins
people.life: b. 12 Jul 1850 Oshawa, Ontario (Pear p. 59; Book of Detroiters 1908) or 25 Jul 1850 (Detroit Historical Society); d. 1923, Detroit; buried Elmwood Cemetery
people.role: Co-founder and business partner; dental-supply dealer and maker of Revelation kilns (H. J. Caulkins & Co., 44-46 Gratiot Ave.); ran the business side and the kilns; joint owner of the pottery 1907-1923; president of Pewabic Pottery Co. by 1908
people.notes: Came to Detroit 1871 (George Peck & Co. dry goods); dental supplies from 1877. Married (1) Frances Leadbetter, (2) Minnie F. Peck, 1888. Lived at 74 Edmund Place next to the Perrys (Pear p. 59), later 188 Parker Avenue (wedding of 1918).

people.name: Minnie Peck Caulkins
people.role: Horace's second wife; half owner after 1923, mostly a silent partner; vice-president of the 1929 corporation (Pear p. 233)
people.notes: Gave her half interest to her son Henry L. Caulkins on June 24, 1924 (Pear p. 60).

people.name: Henry L. Caulkins
people.role: Son of Horace and Minnie; secretary-treasurer of the 1929 corporation; half owner from 1924; inherited Mrs. Stratton's 51 percent in 1961 and became sole owner; gave the pottery to Michigan State University (1966 or 1967)
people.notes: Supported the 1978 rescue with his sister Esther Ford (Catallo p. 96).

people.name: Ruth Stone Caulkins
people.role: Named vice-president of the corporation in a warranty deed of June 1, 1929
people.notes: Pear p. 233 names Minnie Peck Caulkins as vice-president instead.

people.name: William Buck Stratton
people.life: b. 16 Feb 1865 Newfield, N.Y. (Pear) / 1864 Ithaca (Catallo) / 1867 (NR 1984); d. 12 May 1938 (Pear) or 14 May 1938 (Catallo), Detroit
people.role: Architect (Stratton & Baldwin) of the pottery building (1906-07) and its 1911-12 addition; husband of Mary Chase Perry from 1918; designed pieces and threw on the wheel at Pewabic
people.notes: Pear p. 84: many pieces he threw at Pewabic 'have become choice collector's pieces'; Pear figs. 133-137 show vases 'designed and modelled by William B. Stratton. Executed at Pewabic Pottery.' Lehner p. 342 (citing Evans 1974 p. 229) says 'WBS' may be found on early pieces. Cornell B.S. Architecture 1888; to Detroit 1889 (Pear p. 79). The Detroit Institute of Arts trustee 1914-1938.

people.name: Frank C. Baldwin
other_names: Frank D. Baldwin (the National Historic Landmark nomination 1991)
people.life: 1869-1945 (title of a typescript cited in NR 1971 bibliography)
people.role: Stratton's architectural partner; co-architect of the pottery building
people.notes: MIT 1890 (NR 1984). Middle initial differs: 'Frank D.' (the National Historic Landmark nomination 1991) vs 'Frank C.' (NR Stratton House 1984) vs 'Frank Conger Baldwin, 1869-1945' (NR 1971 bibliography).

people.name: Charles Lang Freer
people.life: b. 25 Feb 1856 Kingston, N.Y.; d. 25 Sep 1919
people.role: Patron and collector; challenged Perry to recreate iridescent glazes; bought Pewabic for his collection (now the Freer Gallery); introduced architects (e.g., Ralph Adams Cram)
people.notes: Pear p. 68 says Pewabic is the only American pottery in the Freer Gallery. Earliest dated purchase in Pear: May 1, 1909 (iridescent, $17). He gave three pieces to the Detroit Museum of Art in 1913.

people.name: Charles Fergus Binns
people.role: Director of the ceramics school at Alfred; Perry's teacher (summer 1900/1901/1902)

people.name: Frank Burley
people.role: Head of Burley & Company, Chicago china and lamp house; first large customer (1903, $1,000 order); urged a trade name and chose 'Pewabic' from Perry's list

people.name: Alanson Fox
people.role: Owner of the stable on Alfred Street that became the first workshop
people.notes: The National Historic Landmark nomination 1991 instead calls it the carriage house 'behind the Cornelia S. Fox mansion on Alfred Street'; Catallo and Pewabic put it behind the Ransom Gillis house.

people.name: Julius Albus
people.role: First employee (aged 12): washed mills, weighed glazes and loaded the glaze mills; made tiles with Heerich; threw on the wheel; later general supervisor/foreman of the works and of major installations; kept glaze records; Douglas (via Catallo) calls him the glazeman who glazed and fired student work
people.notes: Son of one of Caulkins' workmen. Supervisor 'until 1940' (Pear p. 207). Led installations including the Pierce Mausoleum, Buffalo (1911) and the Detroit Public Library loggia mosaic. Pear figs. 457, 459 show him throwing; a Dec. 1922 magazine credits a large garden vase 'designed and made by him' (Pear p. 207). His own pieces are not separately marked (Pear p. 161).

people.name: Joseph Heerich
other_names: Joseph Herrick (the National Historic Landmark nomination 1991)
people.life: 1853-1938 (Pear p. 211, Catallo p. 91, The Henry Ford); Pear's chapter heading says 1853-1937
people.role: Master potter and thrower: threw the vessel forms from Perry's drawings on a kick wheel; also worked the jigger; made the building's floor tiles with Albus
people.notes: Born in Alsace-Lorraine (Pear p. 210 prints the town as 'Zarburg', unverified); to the US 1881, Detroit 1891 (Pear p. 211); found cleaning Pullman cars at the Michigan Central depot. Pear p. 211: 'more than a million pieces'. Many Pear captions read 'Thrown by Joseph Heerich'. Pear p. 210 says he stamped his pieces 'Revelation Pottery' with M.C.P., then from 1903 the 'Pewabic Pottery' seal - the seal is the pottery's, not his. The Henry Ford: Stable-studio vases 1903-1907 have 'forms thrown by potter Joseph Heerich ... and applied decoration and glazing by Mary Chase Perry'. Lived at 1161 Holcomb with Ender. Buried Mount Olivet.

people.name: Joseph Ender
people.life: b. 1885 Breslau, Germany (Pear p. 213); d. Aug 1959 aged 74 (Catallo p. 92)
people.role: Kiln man and clay worker: stacked and fired the kilns, ran the blunger, ground grog, tended the glaze mills; maintenance; repaired installations in the field
people.notes: Heerich's nephew. Married Mary Bezold Feb 1915. Tiles made by him and Heerich are in his family's (Blake) collection (Pear p. 213) - family provenance is the only way to tie pieces to him.

people.name: Louis Tomasi
people.life: b. 23 Sep 1885 Vione, Italy (Pear p. 215); d. 1961
people.role: Trained potter (studied pottery in the Tyrol, Austria); potter and installer of tile and mosaic
people.notes: Returned to Italy 1919-1922 (Pear p. 215). Installed: Pierce Mausoleum, Buffalo; Pennsylvania Hotel, New York; Fisher Arcade, Union Trust (Guardian) Building, Stroh Brewery and Detroit Public Library (Pear p. 215). Holden 1926 mentions 'a picturesque old potter from Austria, skilful at the wheel' without a name - possibly Tomasi, possibly Graziosi; not established.

people.name: John Graziosi
people.life: b. 26 Sep 1884 Edolo, Italy; d. 15 Jul 1957
people.role: Thrower and installer; could 'throw or mold a pot blindfolded'; demonstrated throwing for J. L. Hudson Co.
people.years: about 1910/1913-1957 (47 years according to Pear and Catallo)
people.notes: Trained at the Tomasi Brothers' pottery, Edolo. Listed among Day Book workers 1907-1913 (Pear p. 161). On pieces he threw for himself at home (own wheel and kiln) he signed 'John' (Pear p. 161, p. 217) - the only individual potter's signature Pear records.

people.name: Peter Karrar
people.role: Tile layer (Day Book 1907-08, $9.00/week); later ran the filter press
people.notes: From Florence, Italy (Pear p. 149).

people.name: Arthur Kay Herbert
people.role: Modeller and draughtsman: modelled frames for wooden molds; drew the Stations of the Cross for the National Shrine crypt

people.name: Margaret Brandon
people.role: Led volunteer mosaic layers (Oberlin loggia, about 1917); modeller on the Shrine Stations of the Cross

people.name: Henry Albertina
people.role: Modeller, Shrine Stations of the Cross

people.name: Virginia Gies
people.role: Designer and sculptor (e.g., Kirk-in-the-Hills panels)

people.name: Gwen Lux
people.role: Protégée; sculptor and designer who worked part-time at Pewabic from her mid-teens; resident artist in the Strattons' Three Mile Drive house
people.years: about 1920s-1930s; again works executed at Pewabic in the 1940s
people.notes: Pieces executed at Pewabic include the Detroit Institute of Arts cherub fountain and the Sacred Heart Academy plaque (Pear p. 222). 1933 Guggenheim fellow.

people.name: Alexis Lapteff
people.life: b. 1906 Ufa, Russia (Pear p. 224); death not found
people.role: Designer and sculptor at Pewabic (tile designs, e.g., the Detroit Public Library Storybook fireplace of 1926; 'Attila' for Albert Kahn 1932-33); lived with the Strattons; co-heir of Mrs. Stratton's belongings
people.notes: Training disputed: University of Michigan B.S. Architecture 1930 (Pear p. 224) vs 'Yale-trained architect' (Catallo p. 83). Left in 1935 for General Motors' design section (Pear p. 225).

people.name: Ella Peters
people.life: b. 9 Nov 1901 Mills, Mich. (Pear p. 230); death not found
people.role: Office secretary and bookkeeper to Mrs. Stratton; after 1961 general manager who completed the final installations and kept orders going
people.notes: Pear p. 217: she could identify who worked on which installations after 1938. Lent the Stratton papers microfilmed by the Archives of American Art (reel 593, per AAA summary seen in search). End date: Feb 1969 (Pear p. 231) vs 1966 (Fisher p. 75).

people.name: Florence Austin Barnum
people.life: b. 8 Feb 1888 Eagle Lake, Ontario; d. 1966 (Pear p. 228-230)
people.role: Companion and nurse to Mrs. Stratton in her last years; co-heir of her belongings

people.name: Mrs. E. Clingman
people.role: Carried out special glaze tests

people.name: Benjamin March
people.role: Detroit Institute of Arts curator of Asiatic art (1927-31) who demonstrated in the Pewabic workshop one day a week

people.name: Murray Douglas
people.role: Student in the Wayne classes at Pewabic (1936) and associate about 1935-1942; his 1986 letter (Cranbrook Archives) is Catallo's main source on the 1930s staff and the Michigan State changes

people.name: Day Book workers, Nov 1907-Dec 1913
people.role: Workers named in the Pewabic Day Books (roles not given, apart from Heerich, Albus and Karrar, who have their own entries; Ender, Tomasi and Graziosi are also on the list)
people.years: at some time between Nov 1907 and Dec 1913
people.notes: List read from the page image of Pear p. 161 (the OCR scrambles the columns). Pear says 53 different workers; some first names were omitted in the Day Books. Mary Ender is listed under her married name although she married Joseph Ender in 1915 (Pear p. 213). 'Marion Loud' may be Marian V. Loud, who wrote the 1911 Handicraft article on the St. Paul's Cathedral floors - not established.

people.name: Unnamed 1926 staff
people.role: Staff as listed in 1926: an old Austrian potter at the wheel, a foreman, three women pasting mosaics, two fire-tenders and clay mixers, a bookkeeper and an assistant designer
people.notes: Shows women worked in mosaic; Catallo p. 105 (archivist Kimmie Dobos) says Stratton hired women partly for their nimble fingers.

people.name: Roger Ault
people.role: Director of Pewabic Pottery for Michigan State University; planned the museum selection; author of The Collector Looks at Detroit (1973)
people.notes: Start and end dates not found.

people.name: James Powell
people.role: Instructor (Michigan State); taught daily adult-education classes at the pottery; salt-glaze potter (Michigan State gallery show Mar 7-May 1, 1976)
people.notes: Cranbrook M.F.A. (Pear p. 233).

people.name: Primo Volloni
people.role: General maintenance and repair work (Michigan State era)

people.name: Thomas W. Brunk
people.role: Curator and archivist of Michigan State's Pewabic Pottery; co-founder of the Pewabic Society (1979) and its president 1988-1989; author of Pewabic Pottery: Marks and Labels (1978) and the 2021 Michigan State Press history

people.name: C. Allan Harlan
people.role: Detroit industrialist and former Michigan State trustee; gave $35,000 for the building's rehabilitation and helped Michigan State acquire it

people.name: Raymond Vlasin
people.role: Dean (Michigan State continuing education/Lifelong Education) who handed the pottery to the Pewabic Society

people.name: David McKeehan
people.role: President of the Pewabic Society during the 1979-81 transfer; wrote the 1982 grant to convert the attic into studios

people.name: Virginia Ryan
people.role: President, Board of Trustees, Pewabic Society, Inc.
people.notes: Addressee of NPS letters July 1991 and May 1992.

people.name: Ronald Streitz, Jr.
people.role: Interim executive director, Pewabic Society

people.name: Melanie Bazil
people.role: Archivist at Pewabic Pottery

people.name: Terese Ireland
people.role: Executive director (as of 2003)
people.notes: Seen only in a search-engine snippet of the Detroit Jewish News, July 4, 2003 ('says Ireland, Pewabic's executive director'); the page itself is behind a bot check and was not read. Treat as a lead.

people.name: Steve McBride
people.role: Former studio potter at Pewabic; executive director
people.years: potter (dates not found); executive director about 2015-30 Sep 2025
people.notes: Led the 2018-19 tile studio, courtyard and equipment projects (Pewabic 2025).

people.name: Jim Leija
people.role: Executive director

people.name: Sherlyn Hunter
people.role: Started in the mid-1980s as a Detroit Public Schools student working as a presser; fabrication supervisor by 2017

people.name: Anat Shiftan
people.role: Chief designer

people.name: Diana Pancioli
people.role: Eastern Michigan University ceramics professor and Pewabic employee during the People Mover work; later public works ('Arc' 1996, 'Passage' 2003)

people.name: Tom Phardel
people.role: Instructor at Pewabic; People Mover station artist

people.name: David McGee
people.role: Senior designer

people.name: Alex Thullen
people.role: Glaze development specialist

people.name: Neil Laperriere
people.role: Kilns (including iridescent firing)

people.name: Chris Mayse
people.role: Kilns

people.name: Kimmie Dobos
people.role: Archivist

people.name: Nicole Marocco
people.role: Thrower (photo caption)

people.name: Genevieve Sylvia
people.role: Designer (2001 Detroit Metro Airport job; design team tile showroom)
people.notes: Catallo does not state her employer; a 2025 comment on Pewabic's site signed by her refers to 'the Design team's Tile-showroom'.

places.name: Perry birthplace and childhood home
places.address: Hancock Street, Hancock, Houghton County, Michigan (street number not found)
places.notes: Dr. Perry rented, then bought, the house from Ransom Shelden; his office was in the right wing. NPS says the childhood home still stands. Near the Pewabic copper lode/mine (Pewabic and Quincy Mining Co.).

places.name: Perry family house, Edmund Place
places.address: Edmund Place, Brush Park, Detroit (next door to the Caulkins family at 74 Edmund Place)
places.notes: Caulkins' basement was the first test lab.

places.name: China-painting studio, 6 West Adams
places.notes: Shared with three other women (Misses Leonard, Candler and Isbell according to Pear p. 59).

places.name: H. J. Caulkins & Co. (Revelation kilns)
places.address: 44-46 Gratiot Avenue, Detroit (Perry's listed address 1900-02); later the Capitol Park Building (Pear)
places.notes: Pear p. 19 OCR reads '24 Gratiot Avenue' - not image-checked.

places.name: The Stable Studio (first workshop)
places.address: Carriage house/stable on Alfred Street at John R Street, Brush Park, Detroit; Pear p. 34: '83 Alfred Street'; Pear p. 171: 'corner of John R and Alfred Streets'
places.notes: Owner Alanson Fox; rent $8 a month payable quarterly. Behind the Ransom Gillis house (Catallo, Pewabic) or 'behind the Cornelia S. Fox mansion' (the National Historic Landmark nomination 1991). A lead (Boston Society of Arts and Crafts exhibition record, 1981, search snippet only) gives '276 John R St., Detroit (1907)' - not verified.

places.name: Pewabic Pottery building
places.address: 2161 Jefferson Avenue (East), Detroit, at Hurlbut Street, opposite Water Works Park (1907-about 1920s numbering); now 10125 East Jefferson Avenue, Detroit 48214
places.notes: Stratton & Baldwin, Tudor Revival/Kentish inn: brick ground floor, half-timbered stucco upper floor, hip roof, two chimneys; 300-ft-deep lot (50 ft of Lot E + 30 ft of Lot D, Water Works Subdivision, Private Claim 257). Original foundation 76 ft 9 in x 48 ft 10 in; extension made it 103 ft long (Pear p. 60, 233). Original clay-making machine (1912) and dumbwaiter still used (the National Historic Landmark nomination 1991). Address change from 2161 to 10125: the date of Detroit's renumbering was not established here; Pear notes 1917 letters still addressed '2161 Jefferson Avenue, East'.

places.name: 1911-12 rear addition
places.address: Rear of the Jefferson Avenue building
places.notes: Two-story factory addition: blunger, filter press, pug mill (clay mixer), tile pressing and glazing, upstairs layout and storage space; replaced a small 'Crossley clay outfit' in the basement.

places.name: Maxine and Stuart Frankel Foundation Pewabic Tile Studio
places.address: Behind the historic building, 10125 East Jefferson Avenue
places.notes: 2,500 sq ft, $1.1 million; mold making and tile pressing. Catallo (2017) also mentions 'a neighboring building' and 'an offsite vessel-throwing studio' (single-source; addresses not found).

places.name: W. B. Stratton's bachelor house
places.address: West Warren Avenue, Detroit (number not found)

places.name: Mary Chase Perry's house, 138 East Grand Boulevard
places.years: built 1912 for Perry; the Strattons' home 1918-1927/28; dismantled 1927 and its materials reused at Three Mile Drive
places.notes: Its fireplace was the first tile fireplace Perry made (Pear p. 29).

places.name: Caulkins house, 188 Parker Avenue
places.notes: Site of the Perry-Stratton wedding, June 19, 1918.

places.name: Stratton House
places.address: 938 Three Mile Drive, Grosse Pointe Park, Michigan (Lot 10, Henry Russel's Three Mile Drive Subdivision)
places.years: built 1927 (Pear: 1928); the Strattons' home to 1937; NR-listed (NRIS 84001867)
places.notes: Pewabic tile throughout (roof of unglazed Pewabic tile; iridescent blue fireplace surround and baths); garden fountain with duplicates of the 1911 Freer fireplace tiles; Spanish pillars bought 1924. Resident artists Gwen Lux and Alexis Lapteff. Catallo's bibliography URL slug reads '936' - the NR form says 938.

places.name: 134 East Grand Boulevard
places.notes: Pear Fig. 82; Catallo says they moved 'back to Grand Avenue' in 1937 without a number.

places.name: Last home, Cadillac Avenue
places.address: 1370 Cadillac Avenue, Detroit (a few doors from the pottery)

places.name: Graves
places.address: Greenwood (Historic) Cemetery, Birmingham, Michigan (Mary Chase Perry Stratton and W. B. Stratton); Elmwood Cemetery, Detroit (Horace J. Caulkins, under a monument designed by Perry Stratton; also Julius Albus)

places.name: Workers' homes
places.address: Albus: 3375 Hendricks Street; Heerich and Ender: 1161 Holcomb; Graziosi: Kerwin (later Bewick Avenue), then McCormick Avenue with a basement kiln and wheel; Tomasi: Georgia Avenue - all Detroit
places.notes: Graziosi's home kiln matters: pieces he made there are signed 'John' and are not Pewabic products (Pear p. 161, 217).

glazes.name: Early matte enamels (the original 'Pewabic ware' glazes)
glazes.date_note: Earliest bowls with matte glaze were marked 'Perry' in the Stable-Studio (Pear). First printed descriptions are Barber 1904 and Keramic Studio Feb 1905. Never dropped: matte glazes sit beside the iridescents in the 1930s and in the modern palette. The the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination treats the matte glazes as the pre-1909 phase only.
glazes.looks: Thick, opaque, non-glossy enamel that comes from the kiln with a natural matte finish; relief leaf decoration is common; colors run through greens, purples, yellows, with orange-yellow streaked brown singled out as her best. Perry's own press called the tints 'like ice in the sunshine or of the dead gold of Autumn leaves' (The Craftsman).
glazes.tell_apart: Grueby-style matte greens were everywhere in 1903-05; Keramic Studio said Perry's yellows, buffs and browns were what set her apart from 'the eternal mat greens'. Look for the impressed PEWABIC mark (leaf row in the earliest) rather than judging glaze alone.

sources.where: vol. 7, Detroit Arts and Crafts exhibition notice

disagreements: Start date. Pear: matte-glazed bowls marked 'Perry' in the Stable-Studio before the name 'Pewabic' (Pear dates the name 1903, p. 28 and p. 34 gives 1905 for the same event). Pewabic timeline: lamps and vases from 1900. The the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination says the pre-iridescent matte period ran 'until 1907'.

glazes.name: Dull green matte
glazes.date_note: The 1903 Burley & Co. order (Chicago, $1,000) was filled in dark green matte, 'the only color we had' (Catallo quoting Stratton). Pewabic's own timeline: 1903 dark green glazed bowls and jars to Burley.
glazes.looks: A low-luster, earthy green; Barber says the dull green enamel has a tone quality 'entirely different from that of any other ware'.
glazes.tell_apart: The color was popularized by Grueby (Paris 1900 prize); Pear and Catallo both say Perry made it to meet the demand. A green matte vase is therefore the least distinctive Pewabic glaze; rely on the base mark, impressed or paper label.

glazes.name: Orange-yellow matte streaked with brown
glazes.date_note: Barber 1904 (written about the first years of production) says this is where Perry achieved 'her greatest success'.
glazes.looks: An orange-yellow ground streaked 'with warm, rich browns'; Keramic Studio adds that buffs and browns read as a unit with the form.
glazes.tell_apart: Not a glaze other Arts and Crafts potteries sold under this description in the two period sources; no comparison tested.

glazes.name: Flow or trickle glazes
glazes.date_note: Described in print 1904-05. Pear's illustrations include a gold-tone vase with an off-white drip (Fig. 401) and Stratton's own note on a jar given to San Diego: 'lead glaze and alkaline dripper with copper oxide'. No end date: drips occur in later iridescent and matte work.
glazes.looks: A heavy enamel of one or more colors trickles down the sides over a ground of a different tint, 'suggestive of some of the slow flowing glazes of Oriental wares' (Barber). Combinations named: yellow and brown, or blue, purple and white.
glazes.tell_apart: Genuine drips are thick, pooled at the foot and partly stop above the base; the base mark still decides. Keramic Studio's plate caption calls the effect 'FLOWING MAT GLAZES'.

sources.where: p. 219, plate caption 'FLOWING MAT GLAZES - MARY CHASE PERRY'

glazes.name: Crystalline spots and natural crystallizations
colors: light spots on a uniform ground
glazes.date_note: Mentioned by Barber 1904 and Keramic Studio 1905 for the early matte ware. Pear also describes copper glazes that 'broke into tiny crystallizations' with a pebbled surface (p. 44) in the iridescent experiments.
glazes.looks: Light-colored crystalline spots scattered evenly through a uniform ground color (Barber); 'unexpected natural crystallizations' (Keramic Studio); a pebbled faceted surface sparkling in many hues (Pear on the copper experiments).
glazes.tell_apart: This is NOT the large-flower macro-crystalline glaze of Robineau or Teco. Pear's 'Other Experiments in Crystalline and Iridescent Glazes' chapter (p. 245 ff.) is about other potters (John Foster, Robineau), not Pewabic. No source says Pewabic made macro-crystalline ware.

glazes.name: Crackle (craquelle) glaze on a buff body
glazes.date_note: Pear ties the buff body with crackled glaze to the move into the Jefferson Avenue building (1907) and the Arthur Dow dishes for Teachers College, Columbia. A 1930s flyer still offers 'larger jars with craquelle and matt glazes' ($4 to $10).
glazes.looks: A fine network of intentional glaze cracks over a buff body; Dow specified 'a buffish body with a crackled glaze, with a broad band of grayish green around the rim'.
glazes.tell_apart: Intentional crackle is even and fine; later accidental crazing on a non-crackle piece is irregular and can stain. The Griswold Hotel bar tiles (about 1907-11) came out of the kiln with glaze cracks that the owner chose to keep (Catallo).
disagreements: Pear and Catallo both draw on Stratton's own memoir and Pewabic's records; they are not fully independent. No period periodical was found on the crackle glaze.

glazes.name: Egyptian blue
glazes.date_note: The the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination places Egyptian Blue Glaze among the 'traditional matte glazes' she was using before the iridescents (1909). Catallo says she was 'well known' for it. No dated period source found. A dealer page claims it was added in 1911; not used.
glazes.looks: A rich blue matte with depth and intensity of color; where thin it shows an opaline quality, and a second translucent covering 'veiling its intensity' is described. In Stratton's words a 'mellow' blue that broke 'into a thousand refractions of violet'. The Detroit Museum of Art in 1913 described a dull blue bowl with a pearl-like overglaze.
glazes.tell_apart: Do not equate with the shiny dark cobalt of commercial blues. The 1913 museum description is the nearest period evidence of look; test any blue against Detroit Museum's account (dull blue, opalescent overglaze at the rim).
disagreements: Matte vs iridescent: the National Historic Landmark nomination says matte; a modern magazine (The Connoisseur, undated) calls it an iridescent 'Egyptian blue' glaze. Pewabic's timeline lists 'cobalt blue' among the iridescent colors and Pewabic today keeps 'Blue' reserved for architectural tile (iridescent blog).
Date: the National Historic Landmark nomination implies before 1909; a seller page says 1911. No period source dates it.

glazes.name: Blue-and-gold luster
glazes.date_note: End date is the 1912-13 Freer gift documented below, not a production end. Freer's Day Book entry mentions 'a pair of two lustre vases' for $100 (Pear Fig. 420).
glazes.looks: The Detroit Museum of Art (Jan 1913) described a large Freer-donated vase 'in blue and gold that dazzles one with its brilliance and lustre', with 'a most wonderful blue' showing through underneath; Cooper Hewitt's record (about 1909-15) describes a thick blue-green glaze with gold and purple luster at shoulder and neck (record not read).
glazes.tell_apart: Gold luster pools on shoulder and neck, blue shows through underneath. Compare with Weller Sicard, where Barber 1904 says metallic lusters sit on an iridescent ground in painted floral and other designs; Pewabic's metallic effect is in the glaze and is not painted into a pattern.
disagreements: The Brick and Clay Record article reprints the Detroit Museum bulletin, so these two are one source.

glazes.name: Iridescent glazes (the 'rainbow' or luster glazes)
glazes.date_note: Freer set the challenge about 1902 (Pewabic timeline: 1902; Catallo: as early as 1902; the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination: 1903). Catallo: a red copper-reduction bowl 'in probably 1906'. Day Books: first two iridescent sales April 12, 1909 (gray iridescent, to Clara Dyar) and May 1, 1909 (to Freer, $17). Pear dates the climax to spring 1909. First iridescent tile commission: St. Paul's Cathedral, Detroit (floor), first installed about 1909-11. Still made today, in a three-firing process.
glazes.looks: A metallic, mirrored, lustrous skin that shifts color with the light; no two pieces alike; Pear quotes a 1909 reporter on a 3-inch vase with 'a hint of purpling sky', 'a pinkish glow of sunrise'. The Detroit Museum (1913): 'a myriad of elusive gems' playing over a neutral basic glaze. Maker's account: standard glazed pieces are fired twice, iridescent pieces need a third firing, 'fuming', with vegetable oil injected into the kiln.
glazes.tell_apart: Pewabic iridescence is a flash of metal in the glaze itself, built by reduction and fuming; the surface is smooth with irregular color shifts and no painted luster design. Weller Sicard (from 1901 by Barber 1904) and Brouwer's Middle Lane ware (also in Barber 1904) are 'metallic lustre' wares with decoration painted in luster on an iridescent ground. Freer-era Pewabic iridescents are heavy (clay body + thick glaze). Compare with Tiffany Favrile pottery and Rookwood: not checked here (see gaps).

examples.holder: Freer Gallery of Art / Arthur M. Sackler Gallery
examples.accession: 09.255 (per Pear Fig. 91; modern form F1909.255 unverified)
examples.note: Pear Fig. 91 prints this iridescent vase with the accession 09.255. If that is the 1909 acquisition it falls in the first year of iridescents. Not verified in the museum's record.
Vase, ca. 1917, earthenware, credited to Mary Chase Perry. API read; description page not read.

disagreements: When it was achieved: spring 1909 (Pear p. 44; Day Books, first sales April 12, 1909); about 1906 first red bowl (Pewabic timeline: 'delivered a sample in 1906'; Catallo 'probably 1906'); 1910 (Jaqueline Peck, Detroit Women's City Club Magazine, April 1952, as quoted by Catallo PDF 61).

How long it took: about four years from the 1902 challenge (Pewabic timeline and blog); nine years (Collectors News, April 1980, as reported in Lehner p. 342); 'many months and years' (Pear p. 247); the Detroit Museum (1920) dates the experiments from 1903.
When Freer posed the problem: 1902 (timeline, Catallo) vs 1903 (the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination).

Number and names of the 'six colors' (see the color entries): the National Historic Landmark nomination gives rose, green, gold, purple, gold-yellow, copper; Catallo gold, rose, copper, yellow, purple, green; Pewabic timeline cobalt blue, rose, green, gold, purple, copper red; Collectors News via Lehner green, blue, gold, violet, ruby, yellow.

Antecedent: Pear says the 1909 result was inspired by a 'supposed' formula for a thousand-year-old jar read in the Boston Public Library; Catallo says some compared it to Raqqa (Syria) and 14th-century Spanish glazes. Both are stories; no source tests the claim.

glazes.name: Copper and ruby-red reduction glaze
glazes.date_note: Freer told Perry in 1902 she could not produce a ruby iridescence (Catallo). Pear says the first fair example was a copper-reduction piece; Catallo dates 'probably 1906'. Stratton later said copper 'would be the one color' she kept (1951, Detroit News via Catallo). Today the hottest firing, just over 2300 F, produces 'the really saturated copper red' of the holiday season.
glazes.looks: From wine-red with a heavy roll at the bottom edge, 'reminiscent of Sang de Boeuf' (Pear), to bronze or copper with blue or green flashes; the maker's blog shows Copper Iridescent ranging from a sunset-like look to mostly copper with muted blue flashes.
glazes.tell_apart: Same glaze dipped on the same day gave three jars: sea-green, deeper green with gold at the neck, and wine-red (Stratton, in Pear and Catallo): color depends on firing atmosphere, not on a different glaze. Do not use color to date a piece.

glazes.name: Gold iridescence
colors: metallic gold on shoulder and neck
glazes.date_note: One of the six named colors in the National Historic Landmark nomination (gold) and Catallo (gold). Stratton put 'metallic gold' on a jar's shoulder and neck beside a green base (Pear p. 48).
glazes.looks: Metallic gold clinging to the shoulder and neck over deeper green; also used on Chinese-influenced green vases with 'touches of gold iridescence' (Pear Fig. 416); Pewabic's Aurora is today an architectural-only glaze.
glazes.tell_apart: Gold is usually partial (shoulder, rim, high points) rather than an all-over skin.

glazes.name: Rose / pink iridescence
glazes.date_note: Rose appears in the National Historic Landmark nomination list and in Catallo's list and in Pewabic's own timeline. Pear has a 'very beautiful mauve iridescent plate' (Fig. 396). The maker's blog lists a current iridescent called Blush.
glazes.looks: Pink to mauve skin over a lighter body; 'a pinkish glow of sunrise' in the 1909 description.
glazes.tell_apart: Rose and purple shade into each other on one piece (Pear 'mauve'; Collectors News 'violet').

glazes.name: Purple / violet iridescence
glazes.date_note: In the National Historic Landmark nomination list, Catallo's list and the timeline.
glazes.looks: Purple flashes; Cooper Hewitt's blue-green vase shows 'gold and purple luster' at the neck (record not read).
glazes.tell_apart: Often a secondary flash within blue or rose pieces; seldom the dominant color.

glazes.name: Green iridescence
glazes.date_note: In the National Historic Landmark nomination, Catallo and timeline lists; Pear's 'scintillating sea-green' jar (p. 48) and the maker's current 'Matte Green' in the iridescent range.
glazes.looks: A 'scintillating sea-green' from alternately oxidizing and reducing firing (Pear); green vases with touches of gold (Fig. 416).
glazes.tell_apart: Sea-green iridescent is distinct from the dull green matte, which has no sheen.

glazes.name: Yellow / gold-yellow iridescence
glazes.date_note: The National Historic Landmark nomination says gold-yellow; Catallo says yellow; Collectors News (as Lehner gives him) says yellow. Pewabic's timeline omits it and lists cobalt blue instead.
glazes.looks: No physical description found in the sources read.
glazes.tell_apart: Not found.
disagreements: The sixth color is yellow (Catallo, Lehner/Collectors News, the National Historic Landmark nomination 'gold-yellow') or cobalt blue (Pewabic timeline); Lehner lists both yellow and blue but omits copper and rose.

glazes.name: Blue iridescence
glazes.date_note: Pear shows blue and green iridescent vases, a copper and blue bowl and a 'brilliant blue' piece (Fig. 396, 413, 414); the timeline lists cobalt blue; the maker's blog says Blue (and Aurora) is reserved for architectural tile.
glazes.looks: Blue-green skin with gold and purple at the neck (Cooper Hewitt record, not read); 'a blue broke into a thousand refractions of violet' (Stratton quoted by Catallo, about the blue).
glazes.tell_apart: Blue iridescent is distinct from the matte Egyptian blue; the iridescent has the metallic skin.
disagreements: The National Historic Landmark nomination's six colors omit blue; Pewabic's timeline includes it.

glazes.name: Gray and silver iridescence
glazes.date_note: The first iridescent sale in the Day Books (April 12, 1909) was 'grey iridescent'. Pear has lamp bases 'in greens and silver lustres' (Fig. 392). A 1929 fireplace for the Met exhibition used 'raisin and silver' tiles (timeline).
glazes.looks: 'Smoky, delicately iridescent silvery grey sliding into blues' (Murray Douglas, a 1940s student, quoted by Catallo).
glazes.tell_apart: Gray iridescents are easily mistaken for plain gloss under bad light; tilt the piece to see the shift.

glazes.name: Uranium orange
glazes.date_note: Catallo's caption for a 'Uranium Vase, circa 1920-40' only; Thullen (Pewabic ceramic engineer) says some of Stratton's glazes contained uranium and the maker's blog says early formulas included lead and in some cases uranium.
glazes.looks: Bright orange (caption).
glazes.tell_apart: Sources say lead and uranium were used in some early glazes; none says which pieces. Treat bright orange as possibly uranium-bearing; no radiometric facts claimed.

glazes.name: Han-style copper glaze jars (made for Freer)
