glazes.date_note: Freer asked for 'something showing the Han influence'; two jars were made; one went to Louisine Havemeyer and later to the University of Michigan (Emil Lorch bought it as possibly Chinese). Freer died in 1919. No year for the jars in the sources.
glazes.looks: A jar that a Chinese-art collector took for Han; Stratton's note on a lead glaze with alkaline 'dripper' and copper oxide.
glazes.tell_apart: Cases show that museum people were fooled; check base for the impressed PEWABIC.

glazes.name: Raisin and silver (tile)
glazes.date_note: A fireplace of 500+ tiles in raisin and silver, made with Eliel Saarinen for a Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition, 1929 (Pewabic timeline). Pear p. 144 captions a 'raisin and silver' tile design.
glazes.looks: Deep red-purple with silver; the maker's blog says the glaze that impressed Saarinen was her 'forty-second trial' in that color (letter, 1940).
glazes.tell_apart: Documented only for one installation; do not treat as a standard color name.

sources.where: p. 144, caption of the raisin and silver tile design

disagreements: The blog dates the Saarinen/42-trial letter 1940, the timeline puts the Saarinen fireplace in 1929.

glazes.name: King's blue with gold and silver grain
glazes.date_note: The floor of St. Paul's (SS. Peter and Paul) Cathedral, Detroit; Brick and Clay Record, July 1914. Pear dates the commission to Perry winning the job about 1909-10.
glazes.looks: A deep, transparent blue with symbolic figures in grain gold and silver shining up through the overglaze; 'likened to a stained glass window'.
glazes.tell_apart: Specific to the Cathedral; do not expect elsewhere.

glazes.name: Bright (gloss) glazes
also: Staffer glazes in white and cream (as written in Pear's price list)
glazes.date_note: Caulkins's letter of Nov 24, 1907 offered tile 'with half-glaze or all bright glaze if desired' but 'particularly' dull glazes. Pre-1918 price list: single and two-tone glazes in ivory, gray, blue, brown, green; 'all tones of bright glazes'.
glazes.looks: Shiny, even-colored glazes; the 1914 trade report notes 'the blended light and dark blue and light green of Delft ware'.
glazes.tell_apart: Pewabic tile 'has depth and that quality of vibration' (1907 letter) even in plain colors; flat industrial gloss is a flag.

glazes.name: Unglazed and semi-glazed tile
glazes.date_note: 1907 letter: 'tile of unglazed natural clay', or 'half-glaze'. Pre-1918 prices list unglazed green, blue, red and buff-and-brown, with inserts.
glazes.looks: Clay left bare on floors and aisles (Catallo describes unglazed brown tiles in a church aisle, with iridescent accents).
glazes.tell_apart: Floor tile usually carries a small impressed or inked mark; unglazed pieces are the commonest in churches.

glazes.name: 'Peggy blue' tile
glazes.date_note: Named only in Pear's caption to Fig. 414 ('Peggy blue tile') in the author's collection. No explanation of the name.
glazes.looks: Not described.
glazes.tell_apart: Not found.

glazes.name: Modern lead-free palette (post-1983 production)
colors: more than 600 variations in all; giftware under 20; architecture about 70
glazes.date_note: Pewabic timeline: glaze testing for production and sale began in 1983 when Fabrication was reestablished. Catallo (2016-17 text): oxidation firings 2200-2260 F, hottest just over 2300 F; clay and glazes are fired higher and are lead-free, 'matte surfaces that we try to replicate without using lead'.
glazes.looks: Saturated colors with matte surfaces; a modern high-fire stoneware body (ornament pages) rather than Stratton's lower-fired ware.
glazes.tell_apart: Modern pieces are more consistent than Stratton's ('the product today is more pristine', Hunter in Catallo); the base carries the current stamp; ornaments are stamped with the logo on the back (ornament pages).

glazes.name: Pewabic's current Iridescent range (Blush, Matte Green, Copper, Azurite; Blue and Aurora architectural)
glazes.date_note: Maker's blog, undated; Azurite described as the newest. Third-firing 'fuming' with injected vegetable oil.
glazes.looks: Metallic mirrored surface with piece-to-piece variation.
glazes.tell_apart: Modern iridescents are lead-free and uranium-free by the maker's account; do not rely on this alone.

wares.name: Vases, jars and bowls (art ware)
wares.what: Simple graceful forms; leaf relief; small tests and large jars; sold through Arts and Crafts societies on consignment.
wares.recognize: Impressed PEWABIC (see marks topic); the form is usually plain; look for the glaze types in the item list.

wares.name: Lamps and lamp bases
wares.what: Lamp bases with glass shades (leaded shades by Bemis, Detroit; cut glass). Burley order of Nov 28, 1904 lists dandelion, morning glory, cattail and peacock designs. J. L. Hudson's later sold 'gift lamps' with 'heavy pottery vases fired and refired' (undated ad).
wares.recognize: Original shades are rare; check for relief plants that rise into the base; the peacock lamp has tails forming the base.

wares.name: Garden pots and fountains
wares.what: Large garden pots stamped with a big two-inch seal (Pear p. 34); self-watering double flower pots and individual bird baths on bamboo sticks (1930s flyer); drinking fountains and fireplace fountains.
wares.recognize: A large PEWABIC stamp; fountains survive in schools (Southeastern High School 1931 drinking fountain).

wares.name: Field tiles (plain, unglazed, semi-glazed and glazed)
wares.what: Plain pressed tiles with rounded edges and slightly uneven surfaces; unglazed natural clay, half-glazed or bright glaze; 3x3, 4x4 and 6x6 inch modern field sizes pressed by ram press (nine 3x3 at once).
wares.recognize: Rounded edges, slightly uneven surface, slight color variation; architects 'wanted your handmade effect' (Stratton 1946 via Catallo). Modern tiles are crisper.

wares.name: Relief tiles and designed tile sets
wares.what: The three-by-three pinecone tile for a about 1907-10 East Grand Boulevard fireplace (still made, enlarged 6x6); zodiac, children's story, Alice in Wonderland and angel-head tiles; a scorpion zodiac tile around a fireplace.
wares.recognize: Molded relief on a pressed tile; glaze pools in the low parts.

wares.name: Fireplace facings
wares.what: Iridescent fireplace in Freer's Detroit house (1911), the 1929 raisin and silver fireplace for the Met exhibition (500+ tiles).
wares.recognize: Installation-grade: tiles are not marked individually, location and provenance matter.

sources.where: Fig. 111, p. 72; raisin and silver tile p. 144

wares.name: Mosaics
wares.what: Ceramic mosaics for ceilings, vaults and floors in churches and museums (Allen Memorial Art Museum, Oberlin 1917; Detroit Public Library; Basilica of the National Shrine). Not for sale as loose items.
wares.recognize: Small tesserae (not tile) of iridescent and matte colors, gold; loose tesserae of unknown source cannot be attributed.

sources.where: Fig. 430 caption; museum mosaic pieces p. 203

wares.name: Seals, shields, plaques and medallions
wares.what: Business and institutional seals: Albion College 1908, American Blower 'Little Blower' 1907, American Legion, City of Detroit, Union Trust Beehive, Michigan State; 1926 plaques for Christ Church Cranbrook; Kirk in the Hills medallion.
wares.recognize: Rounded plaques with a molded device; sometimes unmarked on the back.

wares.name: Dinnerware
wares.what: Arthur Dow's buff-body crackled dishes for Teachers College, Columbia; replacement china for Women's City Club; Catallo's source says the earthenware 'would chip easily' as daily dinnerware.
wares.recognize: Rare; buff body, crackle, gray-green rim band.

wares.name: Cosmetic jars (Stearns 'Creme Pompadour')
wares.what: The first commercial order in the Stable-Studio, for Frederick B. Stearns Drug Co.; later small square jars with covers pressed from dust, discontinued after a year; shrinkage mismatch of lids.
wares.recognize: Small lidded jars; mismatched lids (matching pairs matter).

wares.name: Buttons, pins and brooches
wares.what: Small jewelry designed by Mary Chase Stratton; became prominent in the Depression.
wares.recognize: Tiny pressed or modeled pieces; check for the mark on back.

wares.name: Depression-era small wares (1930s flyer)
wares.what: Jars for debutante gifts $1-2; larger craquelle and matte jars $4-10; zodiac birthday favors 40 cents; Alice-in-Wonderland panels $3; porringers with bunny handles; ramekins; Madonna plaques $1; octagon tea tile and coasters 50 cents to $1; bird baths; self-watering flower pots.
wares.recognize: Small, low-priced; often the only Pewabic that appears in estates.

wares.name: Giftware: snowflake ornaments
wares.what: Annual trio of ornaments, 3 x 3.25 inches, high-fire stoneware, hand-pressed and glazed, logo stamped on the back; designs from staff each year. Catallo mentions 'annual snowflake ornaments'.
wares.recognize: Dated by the year name on the shop listing; the clay is modern stoneware.

wares.name: Giftware: Postcards from Detroit tiles, Detroit tile/trivet, pint, rocks glasses, classic and petite vases
wares.what: 5 x 7 hand-painted landmark tiles (Belle Isle Bridge first, the Detroit Institute of Arts fifth, Detroit Opera House); a seven-inch round Detroit tile or trivet; the Pewabic pint introduced 2014 in cinnamon; rocks glasses; vases in iridescent, metallic and other glazes.
wares.recognize: Modern current stamp; high-fire stoneware; surfaces cleaner than Stratton's.

wares.name: Commemorative tile for Art in the Stations (Times Square Station, Detroit People Mover), 1987
wares.what: Pewabic's commemorative logo tile given to guests at the 1987 opening; logo by Larry Ebel.
wares.recognize: A logo tile; give as a documented but rare giveaway.

making.name: Clay body: 'hard white'
making.what: Barber 1904: 'hard, white body covered with heavy opaque enamels'. The the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination (citing Evans, Art Pottery of the United States, p. 226, and Brunk) says pieces until 1907 were 'hard white porcelain'.

making.name: Clay body: buff with umber, from northern Michigan
making.what: For the new building, a clay was ordered 'from the northern part of Michigan' with a little oxide of umber; Pear calls it a 'rich buff body'. Dow's Teachers College dishes were specified as 'a buffish body'. Pre-1918 prices list 'buff & brown' unglazed tile.

making.name: Vitrification and firing
making.what: Keramic Studio (Feb 1905): her pottery 'is fired at cone 4 and quite well vitrified so that it holds water'. Barber 1904: fired in the open flame of a muffle kiln without saggers, kerosene as fuel. The Revelation China Kiln could reach 2400 F where standard kilns stopped near 2200 F (the National Historic Landmark nomination).

making.name: Earthenware or stoneware? (museum labels)
making.what: Museums disagree on the same maker: Met vase about 1904 earthenware, 1907-10 earthenware, 1918-25 stoneware (two vases); the Art Institute of Chicago 1926 stoneware; the University of Michigan Museum of Art stoneware; The Henry Ford about 1930 earthenware; Freer 'earthenware' (search summaries).

sources.where: The University of Michigan Museum of Art, Henry Ford, Freer

making.name: Thrown by hand from drawn outlines
making.what: Perry drew outlines and pinned them above Joseph Heerich's wheel; he threw the forms at night; Keramic Studio (1905): one man to throw the forms 'for she uses no moulds'. Large bases were thrown in two parts. A kick wheel and a small electric wheel were used.

making.name: Jiggered, cast and pressed vessels
making.what: A jigger was bought about 1907 for plates for Columbia (molds from East Liverpool); a dust mill pressed the Stearns 'Creme Pompadour' jars (a first commercial order in the Stable-Studio) and later tiles; molds could be of plaster. Pear's clay recipe was meant to be 'thrown on the wheel or pressed in a plaster-of-Paris mould' (Catallo).

making.name: Relief decoration and applied leaves
making.what: Barber: ornamentation 'usually in relief, consisting of natural and conventional leaf forms'. Keramic Studio: 'rather high relief', notably the peacock lamp and flower-growth forms where roots form the base. Pear (Figs. 25, 28-30): early leaf forms thrown by Heerich and designed by Perry.

making.name: Revelation (Caulkins) kiln and the iridescent third firing
making.what: Horace Caulkins's Revelation China Kiln (dental porcelain), bought and sold by Perry from 1896. Iridescents are a third firing with vegetable oil (maker). Pear's account is of repeated oxidizing and reducing firings at 2200 F.

making.name: Tunnel kiln for tile
making.what: A 51-foot tunnel kiln was built; steel trays worked with dark glazes but light surfaces 'became spotted with iron scale'.

reading.text: Barber 1904 describes Weller's Sicard ware (from 1901) as floral and other devices in metallic lusters on an iridescent ground, and Brouwer's Middle Lane ware as 'metallic lustre effects'. Pewabic iridescence is a metallic flash in the glaze itself, built by reduction and a third 'fuming' firing, with no painted luster pattern. The Met says iridescence comes from light reflecting off metal particles in the glaze (search summary; not read); the Freer says it is made by spreading metallic salts such as copper oxides on the pottery before its last firing (search summary; not read).

sources.where: p. 123 (Sicardo-Weller entry); Middle Lane Pottery entry, East Hampton, Long Island

reading.text: Barber 1904 describes Van Briggle as a 'soft, dull glaze' with modeled-in-relief figures (p. 166-167). No source read supports a comparison of Pewabic iridescence with Rookwood or Tiffany Favrile pottery.

Stratton's tunnel kiln trays left 'iron scale' spots on light surfaces; the Griswold Hotel tiles came out with deliberate-looking glaze cracks. Pewabic's early ware had the mark impressed under the glaze, and Evans says heavy glaze can obscure the impressed mark (Lehner p. 342). Photographs of bases belong to the marks topic.

reading.topic: What a collector should not use
reading.text: Do not use earthenware vs stoneware, the exact color of the 'six' iridescents, or the dates for the first iridescent as authenticators; sources split on all of them.

installations.building: Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception (Crypt Church)
other_names: National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception
Immaculate Conception Cathedral (the 1991 National Historic Landmark nomination)
installations.architect: Maginnis (named in Catallo; firm not given in the pages read)
installations.years: 1924-31 (Pear's appendix); Crypt Church used from 1924; about seven years' work per the Shrine
installations.what: Pewabic's largest installation: crypt church ceiling, arches outlined in iridescent tile, large incised ceramic medallions and rondels in the apses, fourteen Stations of the Cross, wall panels; about 35,000 visible tiles combined with Guastavino vaulting (shrine's own count)

sources.where: Sec. 8 continuation pp. 1 and 6: tile installations in 'the Immaculate Conception Cathedral in Washington D.C.'
nationalshrine.org blog pages 'Artist Spotlight: Mary Chase Perry Stratton' and 'The Art of Mary Stratton': largest installation by Stratton's studio; fourteen Stations; Crypt Church first Mass 1924
Appendix II 'Churches, Mausoleums and Memorials', printed p. 284, listed under 1924-31

disagreements: Dates: shrine pages say the Crypt Church and Stations took almost seven years; Pear's appendix gives 1924-31; the Upper Church was finished 1959. No single completion year found.

pieces.provenance: To 1917 Mary Chase Perry Stratton (1867-1961), Detroit, to 1917 [1] From 1917 to 1919 Charles Lang Freer (1854-1919), given by Mary Chase Perry Stratton in 1917 [2] From 1920 Freer Gallery of Art, gift of Charles Lang Freer in 1920 [3] Notes: [1] See American Pottery List, R. 6528, L. 2587, Freer Gallery of Art and Arthur M. Sackler Gallery Archives. According to Curatorial Remark 1 in the object record: "Gift of Mary Chase Perry Stratton in 1946 to replace bowl which was broken. Original bowl [which was a purchase] bearing this number was catalogued as follows: Bowl: tall. Clay: dense, covered with glaze. Glaze: lustrous black mottled with iridescent red-violet. .152 x .143" According to Curatorial Remark 2, S. Hobbs, 1978, in the object record: "This flared bowl with slightly everted foot is a replacement for a very similar piece which was broken and returned to Pewabic Pottery to be fixed. The latter bowl was lost, so the Pottery made a replacement piece. The original was found, repaired and is now in the possession of Mrs. Ella Peters, who was Mrs. Stratton's secretary and her successor at the Pottery until it closed in 1965. ...The original bowl, which Mrs. Peters has, retains the Freer reserve number in red." [2] See note 1. [3] The original deed of Charles Lang Freer's gift was signed in 1906. The collection was received in 1920 upon the completion of the Freer Gallery.

lookalikes.maker: Flint Faience & Tile Co. (subsidiary of AC Spark Plug, General Motors)
lookalikes.why: The look-alike most often named in print. Contemporary Michigan art tile in similar Arts and Crafts and Detroit settings, sometimes in the same installation as Pewabic. Catallo and Pewabic both say Flint Faience tiles are often taken for Pewabic. A documented case: tiles at the old Eastern High School in Lansing were reported as Pewabic in 2025 until Pewabic's archivist said she was 'virtually certain' they were Flint Faience.
lookalikes.tell: Pewabic's guide: Flint Faience was machine-made, so edges are sharper and profiles more precise, and finishes are uniform; Pewabic is handmade, with softer, irregular edges and more variation. Flint's glaze colors differ from Pewabic's historic and current palettes. Flint made continuous raised-line patterns across 6x6 tiles (1926 catalogue) at a precision Pewabic's handmade process did not reach. Flint also made geometric shapes (squares, hexagons) and figurative tiles (fruit, animals, figures). Flint tiles were numbered on the back for assembly (MotorCities). Back marks: not documented.

lookalikes.maker: Rookwood Pottery (architectural faience tile; also art pottery)
lookalikes.years: 1880-1967 (Barber gives 1879 as the founding year); architectural department organized 1902
lookalikes.why: Explicitly confused. The interior lobby-vault tiles of Detroit's Guardian Building (1929) are Rookwood, while Pewabic made the exterior and entrance work, and Stratton coordinated the colors of both firms' work. In 1985 Pewabic made about 1,500 replacement tiles for the lobby, so Pewabic-made tiles in Rookwood designs now sit in that ceiling. Rookwood vessels with tiger-eye or nacreous effects share an iridescent look with Pewabic.
lookalikes.tell: Rookwood art pottery carries the RP monogram, from 1886, with one flame added each year 1887-1900 and a Roman numeral from 1901; each art piece is marked, numbered and dated. Pewabic marks carry no flame dating. Rookwood architectural pieces carry shape numbers with a 'Y' suffix and sometimes a large plain RP monogram on the back; the body is buff and gritty. Tiger Eye has gold crystals under a very glossy glaze on a red body; Nacreous (1915) is on porcelain marked 'P'. Note: Rookwood marks and master molds were revived in the 1980s (Lehner p.383), so check for modern Rookwood too.

lookalikes.place: Tottenville, Staten Island, NY; also Perth Amboy and Rocky Hill, NJ
lookalikes.why: A Detroit tour guide quoted by Metro Times says the Guardian Building's glazed work above the brick is Atlantic Terra Cotta, not Pewabic; Pewabic's work is only on the lower facade. Popular accounts give the whole exterior to Pewabic.
lookalikes.tell: Architectural terra cotta blocks rather than tiles. Marks: not found.

lookalikes.maker: American Mosaic & Tile Co. / Mosaic Tile Co. (Zanesville) at sites Pewabic later restored
lookalikes.place: Mosaic Tile Co.: Zanesville, Ohio. American Mosaic & Tile: not established
lookalikes.why: Fisher's installation list puts non-Pewabic originals inside Pewabic entries: the Liberty Memorial in Kansas City ('embellishments originally by the American Mosaic and Tile Company; restored by Pewabic') and the Thornlea pool at Cranbrook ('original tiles by Mosaic Tile Company, Zanesville, Ohio'). Pewabic restoration tiles there sit next to another maker's originals.
lookalikes.tell: Mosaic Tile Co.: machine-pressed, vitreous inlaid body, scored to imitate tesserae; monogram stamped on the back ('M.T.C. Mosaic tile co.'). American Mosaic & Tile: no information found.

lookalikes.maker: Grueby Faience Co. (later Grueby Faience & Tile Co.; tile line later made by C. Pardee Works)
lookalikes.place: Boston (Revere), Massachusetts; later Perth Amboy, NJ under Pardee
lookalikes.years: Founded 1894, organized June 1897; renamed 1909; tile business to Pardee about 1919-1921
lookalikes.why: Matte green. Stratton's early matte green followed the 'Grueby green' fashion after the 1900 Paris Exposition, and writers have claimed Grueby influenced her (Pear disputes it). Not found named as confused with Pewabic.
lookalikes.tell: Grueby vessels are impressed with a circular 'GRUEBY FAIENCE CO. BOSTON U.S.A.' (the glaze can hide it) and often carry incised decorator initials. Tiles are impressed 'Grueby / Boston' or, in Pardee-era production, 'GRUEBY' with the lotus and hand-painted shape and color codes. Barber 1904 says Pewabic's dull green 'possesses a tone quality entirely different from that of any other ware'.

lookalikes.why: Metallic, iridescent luster on earthenware, the effect Pewabic is known for. Not found named as confused with Pewabic.
lookalikes.tell: Sicardo has painted luster motifs (flowers, vines, scrolls) over an iridescent ground and is signed on the side or face, in the luster ('Weller Sicard', 'W S', 'SICARD WELLER'); the base often has only numbers. Pewabic iridescence forms in the glaze ('not painted on'), and Pewabic marks are on the underside.

lookalikes.maker: Theophilus A. Brouwer Jr., Middle Lane Pottery / Brouwer Pottery
lookalikes.place: East Hampton, then Westhampton, Long Island, NY
lookalikes.years: Pottery opened 1894; Westhampton from 1902/03; Brouwer died 1932
lookalikes.why: Iridescent 'fire painting' and luster effects. Pear devotes part of her chapter on other iridescent experiments to Brouwer. Not found named as confused with Pewabic.
lookalikes.tell: Brouwer used a fast open fire on a biscuit body, giving orange, brown, red and gold tones. Marks: whale jaw-bones enclosing 'M' (impressed according to Barber, incised per the Met and Lehner), 'FLAME', a 'Brouwer' signature, or an incised 'B'. No PEWABIC stamp.

sources.where: p.245 (quoting F.H. Rhead, The Potter, Jan 1917)

lookalikes.maker: Tiffany Studios pottery (Louis C. Tiffany, 'Favrile Pottery')
lookalikes.why: The name: Pewabic's iridescence is popularly likened to Tiffany glass. No source documents Tiffany pottery with luster glazes or names a confusion with Pewabic.
lookalikes.tell: Mostly slip-cast forms with naturalistic plant relief, usually in a semi-matte monochrome glaze. Incised 'LCT' monogram, sometimes 'Tiffany Favrile Pottery' with a P-number.

lookalikes.why: Matte, relief-modelled art pottery, comparable to early matte Pewabic with relief leaves. Stratton owned a Van Briggle jar. Not found named as confused; this comparison is the sub-researcher's inference.
lookalikes.tell: Incised 'AA' monogram, 'VAN BRIGGLE' and, on 1901-1907 work, the year. Hand-incised except the stamped dates 1915 and 1916.

lookalikes.why: Crystal-flecked matte glazes, comparable to Pewabic's early crystalline-spot glazes (Barber). Not found named as confused; this is an inference.
lookalikes.tell: Incised 'Clifton' and a year (e.g. 'Clifton / 1906'), with impressed numbers. Crystal Patina is matte with small crystals, not iridescent.

lookalikes.why: Iridescent luster glazes ('marigold', 'larkspur') in the 1920s. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Incised name on early pieces; later a black stamp 'Cowan' or 'Cowan Potteries', a 'Cowan' circle, or 'R.G.' Red body 1912-17; high-fired porcelain at Rocky River from 1920, so Cowan luster is usually on a white porcelain body (an inference from Lehner and the museum). Marks can wear off or be hidden under felt pads.

lookalikes.years: Art pottery from 1896 to about 1907, then tile; Feroza 1901; Opalesce 1903
lookalikes.why: Metallic and lustrous surfaces. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Impressed 'OWENS' with a shape number, or line names ('FEROZA'). Opalesce is a deposited metal layer over a slip-painted floral design (single museum source). Lehner: 'Much of his pottery is unmarked.'

lookalikes.why: Over a hundred glazes, including luster and crystalline. Stratton owned a Fulper black jar. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: 'FULPER' stamped in a vertical rectangle, or paper labels; mostly molded forms.

lookalikes.why: Arts and Crafts relief tiles (peacocks, birds, foliage) used in the same kinds of fireplaces. Pewabic's design library held Batchelder catalogues. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Non-vitreous body with slip wiped from the high points, a dull non-glossy surface showing buff on the relief. Back marks 'Batchelder / Pasadena' (earlier) or 'Batchelder / Los Angeles' (later), sometimes with numerals; 'Kinneloa Kiln' after 1938.

lookalikes.maker: Moravian Pottery and Tile Works (Henry Chapman Mercer)
lookalikes.years: 1898/99 to 1956 or the early 1960s; county-run revival from 1974
lookalikes.why: Handmade-looking relief tiles in medieval and Arts and Crafts designs. Pewabic kept Moravian catalogues. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Local red clay body, visible on the back, edges and wiped relief; heavy enamel or coloured glazes in dull tones. Marks: impressed 'MORAVIAN' or Mercer's monogram, or paper labels ('A Mercer Tile'). Modern revival tiles are stamped 'MOR' and the year.

lookalikes.why: Hand-made faience mural tiles. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Paper label or shield reading 'FAIENCE / M M CO' and 'MUELLER MOSAIC CO. / TRENTON, N.J.', with design and color numbers.

lookalikes.why: Decorative art tile of the same period. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Spanish and Moorish multicolour designs, often with cuerda seca (black manganese outlines). Marks: not found outside dealer pages.

lookalikes.why: Relief and pictorial art tiles. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Scenic relief subjects (castles, knights, Spanish and woodland scenes). A boxed 'CLAYCRAFT' mark, but many tiles are unmarked (single-source).

lookalikes.why: Shared installations: AETCo floor tile and Pewabic tile were laid together in the Pennsylvania Hotel roof-garden restaurant, NYC (1918). Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Machine dust-pressed, flat body with a molded maker's panel or initials on the back ('THE AMERICAN ENCAUSTIC TILE CO. LIMITED', 'A.E.T. Co.', AETCO); some late tiles unmarked or ink-numbered. Pewabic tiles are handmade with soft edges.

lookalikes.maker: Cambridge Art Tile Works / Cambridge Tile Mfg. Co.
lookalikes.why: Relief art tile of the period. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Glossy enamel over molded relief or intaglio, in Victorian taste. Raised script 'Cambridge' on the back (single-source).

lookalikes.why: Art and floor tile; also made Grueby-line tiles. Pewabic held the 1928 Pardee catalogue. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: 'PARDEE' mark or a circular PARDEE with a ship. Grueby-line tiles made by Pardee carry GRUEBY and the lotus with painted codes.

lookalikes.years: 1916 to about 1930 for art pottery; some tile later
lookalikes.why: Peacock and other art tiles of the period. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Cuenca tiles: molded ridges hold separate glaze colors. Stamped 'California Faience' or a script cartouche.

lookalikes.maker: Mount Clemens Pottery (Macomb County, Michigan): 'MCP' mark
lookalikes.why: A Detroit-area 'MCP' mark that is not Mary Chase Perry. Lehner's mark index lists 'MCP' under Pewabic, Mount Clemens Pottery and Nelson McCoy. Mount Clemens used 'MCP' in a box, including a mark shared with McCoy under joint ownership about 1967-1974. Not found named as confused; flagged because the initials match.
lookalikes.tell: Mount Clemens 'MCP' is a printed box mark on mass-produced semi-porcelain dinnerware and ironstone, often with dishwasher-safe or ironstone wording. Pewabic 'MCP' initials are hand-signed or on the Revelation seal, on early art pottery.

lookalikes.maker: Greenfield Village Pottery / John A. Foster (Detroit)
lookalikes.place: Dearborn, Michigan; Foster also taught at the Detroit Society of Arts and Crafts school
lookalikes.why: A Detroit maker of art glazes (crystalline). Stratton owned four Foster pieces, now in Pewabic's collection. Not found named as confused.
lookalikes.tell: Incised 'GREENFIELD VILLAGE POTTERY' with a year (e.g. 1942). Foster's work is crystalline, not luster.

lookalikes.maker: Work made at Pewabic by others
lookalikes.why: Work made in the Pewabic building, with Pewabic glazes or kilns, by people other than the production staff. Documented groups: (a) Wayne State students 1936-1947, including Murray Douglas, Hulda Creaser and others; their pieces were glazed by Julius Albus with production glazes; (b) WPA Federal Art Project work, e.g. Clivia Calder's 1938 Williams Hall sculpture at Michigan State, made 'using Pewabic's signature blue glaze and kilns'; (c) Michigan State-era instructors and invitational exhibitors (Jim Powell; 20 area potters in 1974); (d) later studio potters who studied there, e.g. Rosalyn Tyge (Starship Studio, Traverse City; studied at Pewabic 1975-1978); 'Bill Pitney and Former Students' shown at Pewabic in 1982; (e) protégés whose designs Pewabic produced (Gwen Lux, Alexis Lapteff).
lookalikes.tell: Studio potters use their own marks (Lehner illustrates them). How student or class work was marked at any period is not documented.

reproductions.what: 'In Detroit, Life is Worth Living' / Old Detroit tile: original about 1910 (Detroit Board of Commerce), reproduced by modern Pewabic
reproductions.when: Reproduction began in the early 1990s with a tile pressed from the original mold; the design was then re-sculpted into a new master mold by Sherlyn Hunter. Still made as a 4x4 in several glazes.
reproductions.tell: Brunk (2007) calls the tile 'the only original known'. A second original came to Pewabic by donation (2025 post), so originals are very rare and most examples are modern. Modern copies carry the Pewabic logo stamp on the back, are in stoneware, and come in current glazes (Peacock, Honey, Lake Superior, Sepia, Celadon). Fine differences between the original and re-sculpted molds are not documented.

reproductions.what: Heritage Collection reissues of Stratton-era vessels and tiles (see modern_reissues_and_dated_lines). Includes the 5x7 Peacock tile with MCP initials on its face
reproductions.when: 1990s to present (Peter Rabbit 1990s; Little Angel Girl 2002; Step Vase 2003; Snowdrop/Lotus/Pinecone/Celtic vases; many tiles)
reproductions.tell: These are legitimate Pewabic products, not fakes, but they repeat historic designs. MCP on the front of the peacock tile does not make it early: check the back for the modern Pewabic logo. Reissued vases are slip cast in white stoneware, with today's glaze names (Elm, Birch, Balsam, Pewabic Green, Winterberry, Sunstone and Matte Green Iridescent). Iridescent reissues are made by fuming in a third firing. Some tiles were re-sculpted with higher relief (Peter Rabbit, Lovebirds), so relief depth can differ from originals.

reproductions.what: Pewabic-made tiles in historic installations by other makers (restoration and replacement)
reproductions.when: 1985 Guardian Building lobby (about 1,500 tiles replacing damaged Rookwood work); Liberty Memorial, Kansas City (originally American Mosaic & Tile); Thornlea pool, Cranbrook (originally Mosaic Tile Co.); Rainbow Fountain, Cranbrook (reproduction tiles, 2003 or 2004); Booth fireplace, Cranbrook (re-created from photographs)
reproductions.tell: A tile in a Rookwood or other maker's design can be a Pewabic restoration tile, and the reverse. Installation location alone does not settle the maker; the back of a loose tile does.

reproductions.what: New tiles from historic molds, and historic tiles reused, in modern installations
reproductions.when: People Mover, Cadillac Center Station (1987): Diana Pancioli combined Stroh brewery field tiles (made 1935-1955), new tiles from 1926 'career' molds made for Northern High School, and a modern match of the Stroh glaze from Stratton's recipe. Fisher's list marks post-1961 installations that 'may include new tiles from historic molds'.
reproductions.tell: Mixed old and new tiles: post-1981 tiles are stoneware with the modern stamp; Stroh and other reused field tiles are historic. Unglazed backs cannot be seen once a tile is installed.

reproductions.what: Imitation of a Pewabic installation by another maker: Kingswood School 'Green Lobby' floor, Cranbrook
reproductions.tell: The original Pewabic floor was replaced by another maker's tile 'to imitate the original' (Fisher); Catallo calls it 'markedly different'. Restoration with Pewabic tile was planned as of 2017. The floor tile in that lobby, as of the sources, is not Pewabic.

reproductions.what: Misattributed installations (published or popular attributions to Pewabic that are wrong or doubtful)
reproductions.tell: Documented examples: (1) the Nebraska State Capitol has no Pewabic tile, contrary to published citations; Pewabic only bid; (2) the reddish tiles in the Detroit Institute of Arts medallions, and tiles in several fireplaces in Fisher's list, are by other potteries that Stratton ordered from; (3) the Guardian lobby vault is Rookwood; (4) Fisher marks with '§' (questionable attribution, 'certainly made by an art pottery contemporary to Pewabic') the Cleveland Museum of Art gallery floor; Hampton Middle School and Mumford High School (Detroit); Central Elementary and Ishpeming High School (Ishpeming); Negaunee Middle School; Ontonagon Elementary; River Rouge Historical Museum floor; and Longfellow Elementary (Pontiac); (5) Eastern High School, Lansing: reported as Pewabic, probably Flint Faience; (6) Brunk notes Pewabic never published catalogues, so there is no catalogue to match tiles against.

reproductions.when: Stratton's own collection (kept for the Pewabic Museum); the 1978 Michigan State-era sale of attic contents; the modern store, which also sells independent artists; exhibitions of other ceramicists in the building
reproductions.tell: Stratton's personal collection held pottery by Rookwood, Weller, Van Briggle, Newcomb, Grueby, Merrimac, Fulper, Robineau, Glen Lukens, John Foster and others, which Pear says was to be displayed in the Pewabic Museum. Pieces 'from the pottery' or 'from the Stratton estate' are therefore not automatically Pewabic. Pewabic's shop sells independent artists' work, and the building shows other ceramicists' work.

reproductions.what: Forged or added Pewabic marks; fakes
reproductions.tell: NOT FOUND. No documented forgery of Pewabic marks or fake Pewabic pottery was found. Documented reasons genuine Pewabic looks 'unmarked': paper labels lost; heavy glaze filling the impressed stamp; a stamp hidden under residue until cleaned (Rago, Roadshow 2013).

salvage.building: James Scott Memorial Fountain, Belle Isle, Detroit (Pewabic tile, 1925)
salvage.years: During a major demolition-and-restoration 'several decades ago'; year not given
salvage.what: The tiles were removed during repairs. Fragments saved by Chuck Kukawka and Bricklayers & Allied Craftworkers Local 2 were donated to Pewabic's museum and are on display.

salvage.building: Northern High School, Detroit (former; 1920s floral-motif drinking fountain)
salvage.what: A tiled segment recovered from a fountain in the former Northern High School was donated to Pewabic's archival collection. The 1926 'career' molds made for Northern's tiles were reused in 1987 for the People Mover.

salvage.building: River Rouge High School, River Rouge, Michigan
salvage.what: A Pewabic drinking fountain marked as rescued, restored or reinstalled; Fisher lists a fountain at Pewabic Pottery as 'from River Rouge High School'.

salvage.building: Seminole Elementary School, Mount Clemens Community Schools
salvage.what: Drinking-fountain backsplash 'slated to be rescued and reinstalled in Seminole's new building in 2003'. Outcome not found.

salvage.building: Gem Theater and Century Club (Twentieth Century Club), Detroit
salvage.what: Drinking fountains (Gem) and bar (Century Club) marked '***' (rescued, restored and/or reinstalled).

salvage.building: Country Club of Detroit, Grosse Pointe Farms; Schulze Elementary (fountains, fireplaces) and Miller Elementary (fireplace surround), Detroit; the Detroit Institute of Arts American Wing and galleries
salvage.what: Elements marked '***' (rescued, restored and/or reinstalled) in Fisher's list.

Historic green field tiles, donated by the Stroh family, were reused in the People Mover Cadillac Center Station (1987), as a backdrop at the Renaissance Center Station, at Detroit Receiving Hospital ('Arc', 1996) and at Compuware headquarters ('Passage', 2003). Fisher lists the Renaissance Center Station: 'historic tiles used in contemporary backsplash'.

salvage.building: Booth house fireplace, Cranbrook, Bloomfield Hills
salvage.what: The fireplace was removed in the 1970s, later restored from photographs; Pewabic re-sculpted its Rabbit tile.
The original Pewabic floor was taken out and replaced by another maker's tile. The fate of the removed tiles is not documented.

salvage.building: Chalmers Motor Company building, Jefferson & Lycaste, Detroit (Albert Kahn, 1907; Pewabic entrance tile)
salvage.what: Pewabic says the building 'has since been demolished'. Whether its tiles were saved is not documented.

Donated to Pewabic's museum in 2024-25 by Howard Israel and Henry Grix. Spare tiles from the commission exist in private hands, so a loose Guardian-pattern tile need not have been removed from the building.

salvage.building: Eastern High School, Lansing (misattributed: probably Flint Faience)
salvage.years: Demolition under way in 2025; salvage not reported
salvage.what: Tiles reported as Pewabic in 2025; Pewabic's archivist said probably Flint Faience. Included because salvaged tiles from this building may circulate as 'Pewabic'.

numbers.what: Prices: dollar amounts on small paper labels, or pencilled in the center of the round Pewabic label (2.50 to 200.00; '10000' on one M1 piece).
numbers.means: Selling price. Not a date, not a shape number.

numbers.what: '#' numbers with a price on labels: #1, #2, #9, #10, #11 (and '#120' on cloth tape).
numbers.means: Not stated by any source. Possibly a stock or list number. Do not use to date.

numbers.what: Four-digit printed numbers on small rectangular white stickers with perforated black-dash borders, often two per piece (2355 + 3588; 2592 + 6533; 5538 above 2289), or painted in orange inside the foot (6523).
numbers.means: Charles L. Freer's inventory numbers (according to Brunk). A sign of Freer provenance, not a Pewabic code.

numbers.what: Pencil numbers on the round Pewabic label: '6537' (Freer F1917.437), '450 14' (F1912.103), '800' (Brunk, about 1908), '188' in red ink (Brunk, late 1920s).
numbers.means: Not stated. 6537 sits in the same range as Freer's inventory numbers (6523, 6533) and may be one; the others may be prices or stock numbers. Unresolved.

numbers.what: M1, M2, M3 on handwritten labels.
A number incised with MCP on an early piece: '701' (the Minneapolis Institute of Art 2000.225.2, about 1903-1907), with '518' in red pigment.
numbers.means: Not stated. No source says Pewabic used shape or model numbers; the red '518' may be an owner's or museum number. One example only.

numbers.what: Years in the mark: '1908' (molded/incised with Pewabic Detroit); WBS with years 1932-1935; 'Scarab Club 1934'; modern tiles with the year on the back (1992).
numbers.means: The year made (but a molded year can repeat on later casts from the same mold).

numbers.what: Glaze names and codes: K-4 (blue), F-99 (black matte), Blue Matte 201, Bough Red, Crude White, Egypt Blue appear in Brunk's labels as glaze names. On pieces: 'TANBA[?] & BLUE' pencilled on a about 1908 vase (Brunk); 'Rose Kiss' inscribed on a 1938-1950 base (the Detroit Institute of Arts F70.209). Students in Pewabic classes wrote glaze names on their bisque for Albus to glaze (Catallo).
numbers.means: Glaze notes. A glaze name written on a base can mean a class or test piece. No source says Pewabic stamped glaze numbers on production ware.
Museum numbers: the first digits are the year Freer acquired the piece (Pear's caption on p. 201 says 'the first two numbers represent the year'). Never on the pot as a Pewabic mark.
Inventory labels of the collectors Dr. and Mrs. Charles W. Creaser, whose Pewabic went to the Detroit Institute of Arts in 1970 (F70 numbers). Not Pewabic.

numbers.what: Shape numbers or date codes on historic Pewabic ware.
numbers.means: Not found. No source describes a Pewabic system of impressed shape numbers, glaze numbers or date codes on Stratton-era pieces.

reissues.what: Heritage Collection: current production of Stratton-era designs, 'recreated from, based on or inspired by' historic work. Each is marked with the modern Pewabic logo stamp
items: 5x7 Historic Peacock Tile: a 1909 design with MCP initials on the FRONT ('the only tile with her mark on the front'). The back carries the modern Pewabic stamp; a hand-painted version is artist-signed
Old Detroit Tile ('In Detroit, life is worth living'), 4x4: see reproductions
Lotus Vase: about 1903 design, re-sculpted by Paul Johnson, slip cast, flowing matte green 'mimicking its historic counterpart'; the original is in a private collection
Snowdrop Vase: 1903 lamp-base design, slip cast; an original returned to Pewabic in 2006
Pinecone Vase: pinecone motif used from 1907; slip cast. Pinecone tile: Catallo's plates show a modern 6x6 enlarged from Stratton's 3x3 (about 1907-10)
Celtic Vase and Celtic Lamp: based on a historic lamp base; slip cast
Step Vase: sketched in Stratton's daybooks around 1960; first produced 2003 for the centennial
Scalloped Candle Holder: a about 1915-1925 design, re-sculpted by Chris Mayse
Peter Rabbit Tile: 1920s school-fireplace design, re-sculpted by Troy Walker in the 1990s because the molds had degraded
Rabbit Tile: from the Booth-home fireplace at Cranbrook (removed in the 1970s, later restored); re-sculpted by Patty Howard
Little Angel Girl Tile: a variation of the 1903 'Little Blower Girl' with wings added; in production since 2002
Two Angels Tile: 'a revised reproduction' drawn from a black-and-white photo of a historic installation

Cat Tile (1926 Schulze School fountain), Rose, Two Flowers and Cactus Flower tiles (Sarah Caulkins Johnson House), Garden Life and Butterfly tiles (Kirk in the Hills, among Stratton's last ecclesiastical jobs), Trickster and Phoenix tiles, Prancing Deer, Bunny, Lovebirds, Egyptian Lotus, Nekhbet and Scarab tiles (1920s designs)
Blessed Virgin Mary Ornament: a 1940s Stratton design, now pressed in porcelain
Bee Necklace and Bee Pin: based on Depression- and WWII-era animal jewelry; now porcelain
Hex Paperweight and Hex Pin: from Stratton's hexagonal glaze tests

sources.where: product texts for each item named, read 2026-11-25

reissues.what: Annual and commemorative pieces with dates or editions
items: Snowflake ornament trio: released every year since 2009, a new design each year, 'only available for a limited time'. The year is part of the product name; whether it is on the piece is not stated. Example years: 2023 Flutter/Diamonds/Tinsel; 2024 Alpine/Kirigami/Snowspire; 2025 Arctic/Pinnacle/Cozy; 2026 Bright/Flourish/Spruce
Twelve Days of Christmas ornaments: introduced 2005, three days a year for four years, completed 2008; designed by Dave McGee
House & Garden Show pieces: e.g. The Belle Isle Bridge Postcard tile, released at the 25th annual show (2015); Celestial Pin (35th, 2025); Dandelion Pin (36th, 4 June 2026)

Anniversary and commemorative pieces: Butterfly Pin (110th anniversary); Solanus Casey tile (2017 beatification); Michigan State Spartan tile and ornament (about 2019); 'Art in the Stations' commemorative logo tile given out at the 1987 People Mover opening (logo by Larry Ebel)

maker.summary: Mary Chase Perry's pottery in Detroit, begun with Horace Caulkins about 1903 and run by her (as Mary Chase Perry Stratton) until her death in 1961. Production ended in the late 1960s; Michigan State University held the building as a teaching center, and the nonprofit Pewabic Pottery has made pottery and tile there again since 1982 or 1983. Its standard mark is a round PEWABIC DETROIT seal; the first pieces carry Perry, MCP, a Revelation Pottery triangle or five leaves over PEWABIC, and modern pieces a round seal much like the old one but with the year in its middle (1992 on a vase at The Henry Ford), often beside a maker's own small stamp; modern tiles carry a year on the back.
cautions: Modern Pewabic is Pewabic too: the same name, the same building, and reissues of Mary Chase Perry Stratton's own designs, some with her MCP initials on the face. A year in the middle of the round seal, or a year or maker's symbol on a tile's back, points to after 1983; today's pottery works in white stoneware, where the old ware was a soft earthenware.
Most historic Pewabic tile was never marked; Flint Faience (Flint, Michigan, 1921-1933) is the tile most often taken for it, and the Guardian Building's lobby vault is Rookwood.
MCP in a printed box is Mount Clemens Pottery's mark on dinnerware, not Mary Chase Perry's.
